knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \( C < \infty \) the following holds. Suppose that \( X \) is a connected subset of a Riemannian three-manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) . Suppose that every point of \( X \) is either the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck or is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Then one of the following holds (see FIG. 4):

(1) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is the union of two \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -caps and is diffeomorphic to one of \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(2) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is a double \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube. This component is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(3) \( X \) is contained in a single \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

(4) \( X \) is contained in a \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube.

(5) \( X \) is contained in an \( \epsilon \) -tube.

(6) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is an \( \epsilon \) -fibration, which itself is a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We divide the proof into two cases: Case I: There is a point of \( X \) contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Case II: Every point of \( X \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck.

Case I: We begin the study of this case with a claim.

CLAIM A.22. It is not possible to have an infinite chain of \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -caps \( {C}_{0} \subset  {C}_{1} \subset  \cdots \) in \( M \) with the property that for each \( i \geq  1 \) , the closure of the core of \( {C}_{i} \) contains a point of the frontier of \( {C}_{i - 1} \)

Proof. We argue by contradiction. Suppose there is such an infinite chain. Fix a point \( {x}_{0} \in  {C}_{0} \) and let \( {Q}_{0} = R\left( {x}_{0}\right) \) . For each \( i \geq  1 \) let \( {x}_{i} \) be a point in the frontier of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) that is contained in the closure of the core of \( {C}_{i} \) . For each \( i \) let \( {N}_{i} \) be the \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( {C}_{i} \) that is the complement of the closure of its core. We orient the \( {s}_{{N}_{i}} \) -direction so that the core of \( {C}_{i} \) lies off the negative end of \( {N}_{i} \) . Let \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) be the boundary of the core of \( {C}_{i} \) . It is the central two-sphere of an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) in \( {C}_{i} \) . We orient the \( s \) -direction of \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) so that the non-compact end of \( {C}_{i} \) lies off the positive end of \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) . We denote by \( {h}_{i - 1} \) the scale of \( {N}_{i - 1} \) and by \( {h}_{i}^{\prime } \) the scale of \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) . By Lemma A. 2 the ratio \( {h}_{i - 1}/{h}_{i}^{\prime } \) is between 0.99 and 1.01 . Suppose that \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . Then one of the complementary components of \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) contains \( {C}_{i - i} \) , and of course, one of the complementary components of \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is the core of \( {C}_{i} \) . These complementary components must be the same, for otherwise \( {C}_{i - 1} \) would be disjoint from the core of \( {C}_{i} \) and hence the intersection of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) and \( {C}_{i} \) would be contained in \( {N}_{i} \) . This cannot happen since \( {C}_{i - 1} \) is contained in \( {C}_{i} \) . Thus, if \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from \( {C}_{i - 1} \) , then the core of \( {C}_{i} \) contains \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . This means that the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i} \) is greater than the distance of \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) by an amount equal to the width of \( {N}_{i} \) . Since the scale of \( {N}_{i} \) is at least \( {C}^{-1/2}R{\left( {x}_{0}\right) }^{-1/2} \) (see (5) of Definition 9.72), it follows from Corollary A. 5 that this width is at least \( 2\left( {0.99}\right) {C}^{-1/2}R{\left( {x}_{0}\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} \) .

Next suppose that \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is contained in \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . Then one of the complementary components \( A \) of \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) has closure contained in \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . This component cannot be the core of \( {C}_{i} \) since the closure of the core of \( {C}_{i} \) contains a point of the frontier of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) in \( M \) . Thus, \( A \) contains \( {N}_{i} \) . Of course, \( A \neq  {N}_{i} \) since the frontier of \( A \) in \( M \) is \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) whereas \( {N}_{i} \) has two components to its frontier in \( M \) . This means that \( {C}_{i} \) does not contain \( A \) , which is a contradiction since \( {C}_{i} \) contains \( {C}_{i - 1} \) and \( A \subset  {C}_{i - 1} \) .

Lastly, we suppose that \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is neither contained in \( {C}_{i - 1} \) nor in its complement. Then \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) must meet \( {N}_{i - 1} \) . According to Proposition A. 11 the \( s \) -directions in \( {N}_{i - 1} \) and \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) either almost agree or are almost opposite. Let \( x \in  {S}_{i}^{\prime } \cap  \partial {N}_{i - 1} \) so that \( {s}_{{N}_{i}^{\prime }}\left( x\right)  = 0 \) . Move from \( x \) along the \( {s}_{{N}_{i}^{\prime }} \) -direction that moves into \( {N}_{i - 1} \) to a point \( {x}^{\prime } \) with \( \left| {{s}_{{N}_{i}}\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) }\right|  = \left( {0.05}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \) . According to Proposition A.11, \( \left( {0.94}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} < {s}_{{N}_{i - 1}}\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  < \left( {0.96}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \) . Let \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) be the two-sphere in the neck structure for \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) through this point. According to Proposition A.11, \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  \subset  {N}_{i - 1} \) , and \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) is isotopic in \( {N}_{i - 1} \) to its central two-sphere. One of the complementary components of \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) in \( {C}_{i} \) , let us call it \( {A}^{\prime } \) , is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . Also, one of the complementary components \( A \) of \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) in \( M \) contains the core of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . As before, since \( {C}_{i - 1} \subset  {C}_{i} \) , the complementary component \( A \) cannot meet \( {C}_{i} \) in \( {A}^{\prime } \) . This means that the \( {s}_{{N}_{i - 1}} \) - and \( {s}_{{N}_{i}^{\prime }} \) -directions almost line up along \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) . This means that \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  = {s}_{{N}_{i}^{\prime }}^{-1}\left( {-\left( {0.05}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . Since the diameter of \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) is less than \( {2\pi }{h}_{i - 1} \) , and since \( {s}_{{N}_{i - 1}}\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  \geq  \left( {0.94}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \) , it follows that \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  \subset  {S}_{{N}_{i - 1}}^{-1}\left( \left( {{0.9}{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \right) \) . Since the distance from \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) to the central two-sphere is at least \( \left( {0.99}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}{h}_{i}^{\prime } \) , It follows from Corollary A. 5 that the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{i} \) is disjoint from \( {C}_{i - 1} \) and lies off the positive end of \( {N}_{i - 1} \) . This implies that the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i} \) is greater than the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) by an amount bounded below by the distance from the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{i} \) to its positive end. According to Corollary A. 5 this distance is at least \( \left( {0.99}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}{h}_{i} \) , where \( {h}_{i} \) is the scale of \( {N}_{i} \) . But we know that \( {h}_{i} \geq  {C}^{-1/2}R{\left( {x}_{0}\right) }^{-1/2} \) .

Thus, all cases either lead to a contradiction or to the conclusion that the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i} \) is at least a fixed positive amount (independent of \( i \) ) larger than the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . Since the diameter of any \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap is uniformly bounded, this contradicts the existence of an infinite chain \( {C}_{0} \subset  {C}_{1} \subset  \cdots \) contrary to the claim. This completes the proof of the claim.

Now let us turn to the proof of the proposition. We suppose first that there is a point \( {x}_{0} \in  X \) that is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Applying the previous claim, we can find a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( {C}_{0} \) containing \( {x}_{0} \) with the property that no point of \( X \) contained in the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) is contained in the closure of the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( {C}_{1} \) that contains \( {C}_{0} \) .

There are three possibilities to examine:

(i) \( X \) is disjoint from the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) .

(ii) \( X \) meets the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) but every point of this intersection is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck.

(iii) There is a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) that is contained in the core of \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

In the first case, since \( X \) is connected, it is contained in \( {C}_{0} \) . In the second case we let \( {N}_{1} \) be an \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) , and we replace \( {C}_{0} \) by \( {C}_{0} \cup  {N}_{1} \) and repeat the argument at the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \cup  {N}_{1} \) . We continue in this way creating \( {C}_{0} \) union a balanced chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks \( {C}_{0} \cup  {N}_{1} \cup  {N}_{2} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{k} \) . At each step it is possible that either there is no point of the frontier containing a point of \( X \) , in which case the union, which is a \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube, contains \( X \) . Another possibility is that we can repeat the process forever creating a \( C \) -capped infinite \( \epsilon \) -tube. By Lemma A. 15 this union is a component of \( M \) and hence contains \( X \) .

We have shown that one of following holds:

(a) There is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap that contains \( X \) .

(b) There is a finite or infinite \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube that contains \( X \) .

(c) There is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or a finite \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube \( \widetilde{C} \) containing a point of \( X \) and there is a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) that is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

In the first two cases we have established the proposition. Let us examine the third case in more detail. Let \( {N}_{0} \subset  {C}_{0} \) be the \( \epsilon \) -neck that is the complement of the closure of the core of \( {C}_{0} \) . First notice that by Lemma A. 20 the union \( {N}_{0} \cup  {N}_{1} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{k} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) , with the two-spheres coming from the \( \epsilon \) -neck structure of each \( {N}_{i} \) being isotopic to the two-sphere factor in this product structure. It follows immediately that \( \widetilde{C} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {C}_{0} \) . Let \( {C}^{\prime } \) be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) . We use the terminology ’the core of \( {\widetilde{C}}^{\prime } \) to mean \( \widetilde{C} \smallsetminus  {N}_{k} \) . Notice that if \( k = 0 \) , this is exactly the core of \( {C}_{0} \) . To complete the proof of the result we must show that the following hold:

CLAIM A.23. If \( {C}^{\prime } \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) , then \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) .

Proof. We suppose that \( \widetilde{C} \) is the union of \( {C}_{0} \) and a balanced chain \( {N}_{0},\ldots ,{N}_{k} \) of \( \epsilon \) -necks. We orient this chain so that \( {C}_{0} \) lies off the negative end of each of the \( {N}_{i} \) . Let \( {S}^{\prime } \) be the boundary of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) and let \( {N}^{\prime } \) be an \( \epsilon \) -neck contained in \( {C}^{\prime } \) whose central two-sphere is \( {S}^{\prime } \) . We orient the direction \( {s}_{{N}^{\prime }} \) so that the positive direction points away from the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . The first step in proving this claim is to establish the following.

CLAIM A.24. Suppose that there is a two-sphere \( \sum  \subset  {N}^{\prime } \) contained in the closure of the positive half of \( {N}^{\prime } \) and also contained in \( \widetilde{C} \) . Suppose that \( \sum \) is isotopic in \( {N}^{\prime } \) to the central two-sphere \( {S}^{\prime } \) of \( {N}^{\prime } \) . Then \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) , a component containing \( X \) .

Proof. \( \sum \) separates \( \widetilde{C} \) into two components: \( A \) , which has compact closure in \( \widetilde{C} \) , and \( B \) , containing the end of \( \widetilde{C} \) . The two-sphere \( \sum \) also divides \( {C}^{\prime } \) into two components. Since \( \sum \) is isotopic in \( {N}^{\prime } \) to \( {S}^{\prime } \) , the complementary component \( {A}^{\prime } \) of \( \sum \) in \( {C}^{\prime } \) with compact closure contains the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . Of course, the frontier of \( A \) in \( M \) and the frontier of \( {A}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) are both equal to \( \sum \) . If \( A = {A}^{\prime } \) , then the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) is contained in the closure of \( A \) and hence is contained in \( \widetilde{C} \) , contradicting our assumption that \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) . Thus, \( A \) and \( {A}^{\prime } \) lie on opposite sides of their common frontier. This means that \( \bar{A} \cup  {\bar{A}}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) . Clearly, this component is also equal to \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) . Since \( X \) is connected and this component contains a point \( {x}_{0} \) of \( X \) , it contains \( X \) . This completes the proof of Claim A.24.

Now we return to the proof of Claim A.23. We consider three cases.

First Subcase: \( {S}^{\prime } \subset  \widetilde{C} \) . In this case we apply Claim A. 24 to see that \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) .

Second Subcase: \( {S}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from \( \widetilde{C} \) . Let \( A \) be the complementary component of \( {S}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) containing \( \widetilde{C} \) . The intersection of \( A \) with \( {C}^{\prime } \) is either the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) or is a submanifold of \( {C}^{\prime } \) diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . The first case is not possible since it would imply that the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains \( \widetilde{C} \) and hence contains \( {C}_{0} \) , contrary to the way we chose \( {C}_{0} \) . Thus, the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) and the complementary component \( A \) containing \( \widetilde{C} \) both have \( {S}^{\prime } \) as their frontier and they lie on opposite sides of \( {S}^{\prime } \) . Since the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) , it must be the case that \( {S}^{\prime } \) also contains a point of this frontier. By Proposition A.11, the neck \( {N}^{\prime } \subset  {C}^{\prime } \) meets \( {N}_{k} \) and there is a two-sphere \( \sum  \subset  {N}^{\prime } \cap  {N}_{k} \) isotopic in \( {N}^{\prime } \) to \( {S}^{\prime } \) and isotopic in \( {N}_{k} \) to the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{k} \) . Because \( {N}_{k} \subset  \widetilde{C} \) and \( \widetilde{C} \) is disjoint from the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) , we see that \( \sum \) is contained in the positive half of \( {N}^{\prime } \) . Applying Claim A. 24 we see that \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) .

Third Subcase: \( {S}^{\prime } \cap  \widetilde{C} \neq  \varnothing \) and \( {S}^{\prime } ⊄ \widetilde{C} \) . Clearly, in this case \( {S}^{\prime } \) contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) in \( M \) , i.e., a point of the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{k} \) in \( M \) . Since \( {N}_{k} \cap  {N}^{\prime } \neq  \varnothing \) , by Lemma A. 2 the scales of \( {N}_{k} \) and \( {N}^{\prime } \) are within \( 1 \pm  {0.01} \) of each other, and hence the diameter of \( {S}^{\prime } \) is at most \( {2\pi } \) times the scale of \( {N}_{k} \) . Since the central two-sphere \( {S}^{\prime } \) of \( {N}^{\prime } \) contains a point in the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{k} \) , it follows from Lemma A. 5 that \( {S}^{\prime } \) is contained on the positive side of the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{k} \) and that the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{k} \) is contained in \( {N}^{\prime } \) . By Proposition A. 11 there is a two-sphere \( \sum \) in the neck structure for \( {N}^{\prime } \) that is contained in \( {N}_{k} \) and is isotopic in \( {N}_{k} \) to the central two-sphere from that neck structure. Let \( A \) be the complementary component of \( \sum \) in \( M \) that contains \( \widetilde{C} \smallsetminus  {N}_{k} \) . If the complementary component of \( \sum \) that contains \( {C}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {N}^{\prime } \) is not \( A \) , then \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) . Suppose that \( A \) is also the complementary component of \( \sum \) in \( M \) that contains \( {C}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {N}^{\prime } \) . Of course, \( A \) is contained in the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . If \( k \geq  1 \) , we see that \( A \) and hence the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains \( \widetilde{C} \smallsetminus  {N}_{k} \) , which in turn contains the core of \( {C}_{0} \) . This contradicts our choice of \( {C}_{0} \) . If \( k = 0 \) , then \( {C}_{0} = A \cup  \left( {{N}_{0} \cap  \left( {M \smallsetminus  A}\right) }\right) \) . Of course, \( A \subset  {C}^{\prime } \) . Also, the frontier of \( {N}_{0} \cap  \left( {M \smallsetminus  A}\right) \) in \( M \) is the union of \( A \) and the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{0} \) in \( M \) . But we have already established that the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{0} \) in \( M \) is contained in \( {N}^{\prime } \) . Since \( A \subset  {C}^{\prime } \) , it follows that all of \( {C}_{0} \) is contained in \( {C}^{\prime } \) . On the other hand, there is a point of the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) contained in the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . This then contradicts our choice of \( {C}_{0} \) .

This completes the analysis of all the cases and hence completes the proof of Claim A.23.

The last thing to do in this case in order to prove the proposition in Case I is to show that \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) , or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . The reason for this is that \( \widetilde{C} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {C}_{0} \) ; hence \( \widetilde{C} \) either is diffeomorphic to an open three-ball or to a punctured \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . Thus, the frontier of \( {C}^{\prime } \) in \( \widetilde{C} \) is a two-sphere that bounds either a compact three-ball or the complement of an open three-ball in \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . Since \( {C}^{\prime } \) itself is diffeomorphic either to a three-ball or to a punctured \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) , the result follows.

Case II: Suppose that every point of \( X \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck. Then if the two-spheres of these necks separate \( M \) , it follows from Proposition A. 19 that \( X \) is contained in an \( \epsilon \) -tube in \( M \) .

It remains to consider the case when the two-spheres of these necks do not separate \( M \) . As in the case when the 2-spheres separate, we begin building a balanced chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks with each neck in the chain centered at a point of \( X \) . Either this construction terminates after a finite number of steps in a finite \( \epsilon \) -chain whose union contains \( X \) , or it can be continued infinitely often creating an infinite \( \epsilon \) -chain containing \( X \) or at some finite stage (possibly after reversing the indexing and the \( s \) -directions of the necks) we have a balanced \( \epsilon \) -chain \( {N}_{a} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{b - 1} \) and a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{b - 1} \) that is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {N}_{b} \) with the property that \( {N}_{b} \) meets the negative end of \( {N}_{a} \) . Intuitively, the chain wraps around on itself like a snake eating its tail. If the intersection of \( {N}_{a} \cap  {N}_{b} \) contains a point \( x \) with \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}\left( x\right)  \geq   - \left( {0.9}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \) , then according to Proposition A. 11 the intersection of \( {N}_{a} \cap  {N}_{b} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and the two-sphere in this product structure is isotopic in \( {N}_{a} \) to the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{a} \) and is isotopic in \( {N}_{b} \) to the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{b} \) . In this case it is clear that \( {N}_{a} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{b} \) is a component of \( M \) that is an \( \epsilon \) -fibration.

We examine the possibility that the intersection \( {N}_{a} \cap  {N}_{b} \) contains some points in the negative end of \( {N}_{a} \) but is contained in \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1}, - \left( {0.9}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \right) \) . Set \( A = {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1}, - \left( {0.8}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \right) \) . Notice that since \( X \) is connected and \( X \) contains a point in the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{a} \) (since we have added at least one neck at this end), it follows that \( X \) contains points in \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( s\right) \) for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . If there are no points of \( X \) in \( A \) , then we replace \( {N}_{a} \) by an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {N}_{a}^{\prime } \) centered at a point of \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( {\left( {0.15}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \cap  X \) . Clearly, by Lemma A. 5 \( {N}_{a}^{\prime } \) contains \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( {-\left( {0.8}\right) \epsilon  - 1,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) and is disjoint from \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1}, - \left( {0.9}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \right. \) , so that \( {N}_{a}^{\prime },{N}_{a + 1},\ldots ,{N}_{b} \) is a chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks containing \( X \) . If there is a point of \( X \cap  A \) , then we let \( {N}_{b + 1} \) be a neck centered at this point. Clearly, \( {N}_{a} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{b + 1} \) is a component, \( {M}_{0} \) , of \( M \) containing \( X \) . The preimage in the universal covering of \( {M}_{0} \) is a chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks infinite in both directions. That is to say, the universal covering of \( {M}_{0} \) is an \( \epsilon \) -tube. Furthermore, each point in the universal cover of \( {M}_{0} \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck that is disjoint from all its non-trivial covering translates. Hence, the quotient \( {M}_{0} \) is an \( \epsilon \) -fibration.

We have now completed the proof of Proposition A.21.

If \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) then \( s\left( {t}^{\prime }\right)  \geq  s\left( t\right) \) . knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Proof. Clearly, for any \( {t}_{0} \) we have \( s\left( t\right)  = s\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for \( t \geq  {t}_{0} \) sufficiently close to \( {t}_{0} \) . Also, if \( t \) is not a surgery time, then \( s\left( t\right)  = s\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) for all \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) and sufficiently close to \( t \) . According to Proposition 15.3, if \( t \) is a surgery time then for \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) but sufficiently close to it, the manifold \( {M}_{t} \) is obtained from \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) by doing surgery on a finite number of 2-spheres and removing certain components of the result. We divide the operations into three types: (i) surgery along homotopically trivial 2-spheres in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) ,(ii) surgery along homo-topically non-trivial 2-spheres in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) ,(iii) removal of components. Clearly, the first operation does not change the invariant \( s \) since it simply creates a manifold that is the disjoint union of a manifold homotopy equivalent to the original manifold with a collection of homotopy 3-spheres. Removal of components will not increase the invariant. The last operation to consider is surgery along a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere. Let \( {F}_{t} \) be a homotopi-cally essential family of disjointly embedded 2-spheres in \( {M}_{t} \) . This family of 2-spheres in \( {M}_{t} \) can be deformed to miss the 3-disks (the surgery caps) in \( {M}_{t} \) that we sewed in doing the surgery at time \( t \) along a homotopically nontrivial 2-sphere. After deforming the spheres in the family \( {F}_{t} \) away from the surgery caps, they produce a disjoint family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) of 2 -spheres in the manifold \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , for \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) but \( {t}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( t \) . Each 2-sphere in \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from the homotopically essential 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) along which we do surgery at time \( t \) . Let \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) be the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }}^{\prime } \cup  \left\{  {S}_{0}\right\} \) . We claim that \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a homotopically essential family in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) .

First, suppose that one of the spheres \( \sum \) in \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Of course, we are in the case when the surgery 2-sphere is homotopically essential, so \( \sum \) is not \( {S}_{0} \) and hence is the image of one of the 2-spheres in \( {F}_{t} \) . Since \( \sum \) is homotopically trivial, it is the boundary of a homotopy 3-ball \( B \) in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . If \( B \) is disjoint from the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then it exists in \( {M}_{t} \) and hence \( \sum \) is homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{t} \) , which is not possible from the assumption about the family \( {F}_{t} \) . If \( B \) meets the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then since the spheres in the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) are disjoint, it follows that \( B \) contains the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) . This is not possible since in this case \( {S}_{0} \) would be homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , contrary to assumption.

We also claim that no distinct members of \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) are homotopic. For suppose that two of the members \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are homotopic. It cannot be the case that one of \( \sum \) or \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) is the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) since, in that case, the other one would be homotopically trivial after surgery, i.e., in \( {M}_{t} \) . The 2- spheres \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are the boundary components of a submanifold \( A \) in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) homotopy equivalent to \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) . If \( A \) is disjoint from the surgery 2-sphere \( {S}_{0} \) , then \( A \) exists in \( {M}_{t} \) and \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) are homotopic in \( {M}_{t} \) , contrary to assumption. Otherwise, the surgery sphere \( {S}_{0} \) must be contained in \( A \) . Every 2-sphere in \( A \) is either homotopically trivial in \( A \) or is homotopic in \( A \) to either boundary component. If \( {S}_{0} \) is homotopically trivial in \( A \) , then it would be homotopically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and this contradicts our assumption. If \( {S}_{0} \) is homotopic in \( A \) to each of \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) , then each of \( \sum \) and \( {\sum }^{\prime } \) is homo-topically trivial in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) , contrary to assumption. This shows that the family \( {F}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is homotopically essential. It follows immediately that doing surgery on a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere strictly decreases the invariant \( s \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex: Proof. Let \( M \) be as in the statement of the corollary. Let \( g \) be a normalized metric on \( M \) , and let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be the Ricci flow with surgery defined for all time with \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) as initial conditions. According to Proposition 18.9 there is \( T < \infty \) such that every component of \( {M}_{T} \) has trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) . Thus, by the analysis above, we see that there must be surgeries that kill elements in \( {\pi }_{2} \) : either the removal of a component with non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) or surgery along a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere. We consider the first such surgery in \( M \) . The only components with non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) that can be removed by surgery are \( {S}^{2} \) -bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) and \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . Since each of these has homotopi-cally non-trivially embedded 2-spheres, if the first surgery killing an element in \( {\pi }_{2} \) is removal of such a component, then, because all the earlier 2-sphere surgeries are along homotopically trivial 2-spheres, the homotopically nontrivial embedded 2-sphere in this component deforms back to an embedded, homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere in \( M \) . The other possibility is that the first time an element in \( {\pi }_{2}\left( M\right) \) is killed it is by surgery along a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere. Once again, using the fact that all previous surgeries are along homotopically trivial 2-spheres, deform this 2-sphere back to \( M \) producing a homotopically non-trivial 2-sphere in \( M \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof of the first statement is by contradiction. Fix \( \rho  > 0 \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) and suppose that there is no \( 0 < h \leq  \min \left( {\rho  \cdot  \delta ,\rho /{2C}}\right) \) as required. Then there is a sequence of generalized Ricci flows \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined for \( 0 \leq  t < {T}_{n} < \infty \) satisfying Assumptions 11.18 and points \( {x}_{n} \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = {T}_{n} \) contained in \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) in \( {\Omega }_{n} \) with boundary contained in \( {\left( {\Omega }_{n}\right) }_{\rho /{2C}} \) with \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) but such that no \( {x}_{n} \) is the center of a strong \( \delta \) -neck in \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) . Form the maximal extensions, \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n}}\right) \) , to time \( T \) of the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) .

CLAIM 11.32. The sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) satisfies the five hypotheses of Theorem 11.1.

Proof. By our assumptions, hypotheses (1) and (3) of Theorem 11.1 hold for this sequence. Also, we are assuming that any point \( y \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Since \( R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = \; {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) this means that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, any point \( y \in  {\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  R\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. This establishes hypothesis (2) in the statement of Theorem 11.1.

Next, we have:

CLAIM 11.33. For any \( A < \infty \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and has compact closure in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Proof. Any point \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) has scalar curvature at most \( {16}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) and there is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( z \) . This means that for all \( y \) with \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {z, y}\right)  < {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) we have \( R\left( y\right)  \leq  {32}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) . Hence, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) , and thus \( {d}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {Q}_{n}^{1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) . This implies that, given \( A < \infty \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \notin  {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right) \) . Since this is true for all \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) , it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {B}_{{Q}_{n},{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . Next, we must show that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, this ball has compact closure. That is to say, we must show that for every \( A \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large the distance from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of the horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) is greater than \( A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2} \) . If not, then since the curvature at the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) goes to infinity for each \( n \) , this sequence would violate Theorem 10.2.

Because \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn, it is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) for a universal \( \kappa  > 0 \) and \( r > 0 \) . Also, because every point in the horn is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck, for every \( n \) sufficiently large and every \( y \in  B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) the flow is defined on an interval through \( y \) defined for backward time \( R{\left( y\right) }^{-1} \) .

This completes the proof that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1 hold and establishes Claim 11.32.

We form a new sequence of generalized Ricci flows from the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) by translating by \( - {T}_{n} \) , so that the final time-slice is at \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} = 0 \) , where \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} \) is the time function for \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Theorem 11.1 implies that, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack  ) \) defined for some \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) for the sequence \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) . Because of the curvature pinching toward positive assumption, by Theorem 5.33, the limit Ricci flow has non-negative sectional curvature. Of course, \( R\left( {x}_{\infty }\right)  = 1 \) so that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is non-flat.

CLAIM 11.34. \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to the product \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h}\right)  \times  \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) , where \( h \) is a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the usual Euclidean metric on the real line.

Proof. Because of the fact that the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) have curvature pinched toward positive, and since \( {Q}_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, it follows that the geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature. In \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) take a minimizing geodesic ray \( {\alpha }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and a minimizing geodesic \( {\beta }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . As we have seen, the lengths of both \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . By passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the \( {\alpha }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \alpha \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) and that the \( {\beta }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \beta \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since, for all \( n \) , the union of \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) forms a piecewise smooth ray in \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) meeting the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) in a single point and at this point crossing from one side of this 2-sphere to the other, the union of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) forms a proper, piecewise smooth map of \( \mathbb{R} \) to \( {M}_{\infty } \) that meets the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{\infty } \) in a single point and crosses from one side to the other at the point. This means that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has at least two ends. Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature, according to Theorem 2.13, this implies that \( {M}_{\infty } \) is a product of a surface with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( M \) has nonnegative curvature, the surface has non-negative curvature. Since \( M \) has positive curvature at least at one point, the surface is diffeomorphic to the 2-sphere.

According to Theorem 11.1, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on some interval of the form \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) for \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) . Suppose that, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( 0 < T < \infty \) . It follows that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is of non-negative curvature and has two ends. Again by Theorem 2.13, this implies that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a Riemannian product of a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Thus, by Corollary 4.19 the Ricci flow is a product of a Ricci flow \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) with the trivial flow on \( \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) . It now follows from Corollary 4.14 that for every \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) the curvature of \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) is positive.

Let \( {M}_{n} \) be the zero time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is the geometric limit of the \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) , there is an exhaustive sequence \( {x}_{\infty } \in \; {V}_{1} \subset  {V}_{2} \subset  \cdots \) of open subsets of \( {M}_{\infty } \) with compact closure and embeddings \( {\varphi }_{n} : {V}_{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{n} \) sending \( {x}_{\infty } \) to \( {x}_{n} \) such that \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology, uniformly on compact sets, to \( {g}_{\infty } \) .

CLAIM 11.35. For any \( z \in  {M}_{\infty } \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \in  {V}_{n} \) , so that \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) is defined. Furthermore, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a backward flow line through \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) in the generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined on the interval \( \left( {-T - \left( {{R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) /2}\right) ,0}\right) \) . The scalar curvature is bounded above on this entire flow line by \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) .

Proof. Of course, for any compact subset \( K \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( K \subset  {V}_{n} \) , and there is an embedding \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \subset \; {Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) compatible with time and the vector field. The map \( {\varphi }_{n} \) defines a map \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n} : K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since the scalar curvature of the limit is positive, and hence bounded away from zero on the compact set \( K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) and since \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, the following is true: For any compact subset \( K \subset  M \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the scalar curvature of \( {G}_{n} \) on the image \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) is greater than \( {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , and hence for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point in \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since having a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood is invariant under rescaling, it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

Next we claim that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We have already seen that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Of course, since \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact, for \( n \) sufficiently large, the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) must either be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We shall rule out the possibility of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, at least for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

To do this, take \( K \) to be a neighborhood of \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) in the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) with the topology of \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) and with the metric being the product of a positively curved metric on \( {S}^{2} \) with the Euclidean metric on \( I \) . We take \( K \) to be sufficiently large to contain the \( {2C} \) -ball centered at \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) . Because the limit flow is the product of a positively curved flow on \( {S}^{2} \) with the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) , the flow is distance decreasing. Thus, for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the subman-ifold \( K \times  \{ t\} \) contains the ball in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) centered at \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) of radius \( {2C} \) . For every \( n \) sufficiently large, consider the submanifolds \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) of \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since the metrics \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) \) are converging uniformly for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) to the product flow on \( K \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large and any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , this submanifold contains the \( C \) -ball centered at \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Furthermore, the maximal curvature two-plane at any point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost tangent to the \( {S}^{2} \) -direction of \( K \) . Hence, by Lemma A. 2 the central 2-sphere of any \( \epsilon \) -neck contained \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost parallel to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factors in the product structure on \( K \) at every point. This implies that the central 2-sphere of any such \( \epsilon \) -neck is isotopic to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factor of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Suppose that \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) . Then \( \mathcal{C} \) is contained in \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Consider the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N \subset  \mathcal{C} \) that is the complement of the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) . Its central 2-sphere, \( \sum \) , is isotopic in \( K \) to the 2-sphere factor of \( K \) , but this is absurd since \( \sum \) bounds a 3-ball in the \( \mathcal{C} \) . This contradiction shows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , it is not possible for \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) to be contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. The only other possibility is that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

Fix \( n \) sufficiently large. Since, for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, it follows from Definition 9.78 that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) we have \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) (this follows from the fact that the partial derivative in the time-direction of the scalar curvature of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck of scale one is positive and bounded away from 0 \( ) \) . It also follows from Definition 9.78 that the flow near \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) extends backwards to time

\[
- {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  <  - {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,0}\right) }\right) ,
\]

with the same inequality for scalar curvature holding for all \( t \) in this extended interval. Applying this for \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) but sufficiently close to \( T \) establishes the last statement in the claim, and completes the proof of the claim.

Let \( {Q}_{0} \) be the upper bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . By the previous claim, \( {Q}_{0} \) is also an upper bound for the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) for any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) . Applying Theorem 11.1 to the flows

\[
\left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) , - {t}^{\prime } - {Q}_{0}^{-1}/2 < t \leq   - {t}^{\prime },
\]

we conclude that there is \( {t}_{0} \) depending only on the bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) , and hence depending only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , such that, after passing to a subsequence the limit flow exists for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0}, - {t}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . Since the limit flow already exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , we conclude that, for this further subsequence, the limit flow exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Now apply this with \( {t}^{\prime } = T - {t}_{0}/2 \) . This proves that if, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , then, after passing to a further subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0}/2,0}\right\rbrack \) where \( {t}_{0} \) depends only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , and in particular, is independent of \( T \) . Repeating this argument with \( T + \left( {{t}_{0}/2}\right) \) replacing \( T \) , we pass to a further subsequence so that the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Repeating this inductively, we can find a sequence of subsequences so that for the \( n \) subsequence the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - n{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Taking a diagonal subsequence produces a subsequence for which the limit is defined on \( ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) .

The limit flow is the product of a flow on \( {S}^{2} \) of positive curvature defined for \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) and the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) . Now, invoking Hamilton’s result (Corollary 9.50), we see that the ancient solution of positive curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) must be a shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) . This means that the limit flow is the product of the shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) , and implies that for all \( n \) sufficiently large there is a strong \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) . This contradiction proves the existence of \( h \) as required.

Now let us establish the last statement in Theorem 11.31. The subset of \( \mathcal{H} \) consisting of all \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) is compact (since \( R \) is a proper function), and disjoint from any \( \delta \) -neck of scale \( h \) since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) . On the other hand, for any point \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) take a minimal geodesic from \( z \) to the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . There must be a point \( y \) on this geodesic with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) . The \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) is disjoint from \( z \) (since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) ) and hence this neck separates \( z \) from the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . It now follows easily that there is a point \( y \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) and such that the central 2-sphere of the \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) divides \( \mathcal{H} \) into two pieces with the non-compact piece disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We suppose that \( \widetilde{C} \) is the union of \( {C}_{0} \) and a balanced chain \( {N}_{0},\ldots ,{N}_{k} \) of \( \epsilon \) -necks. We orient this chain so that \( {C}_{0} \) lies off the negative end of each of the \( {N}_{i} \) . Let \( {S}^{\prime } \) be the boundary of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) and let \( {N}^{\prime } \) be an \( \epsilon \) -neck contained in \( {C}^{\prime } \) whose central two-sphere is \( {S}^{\prime } \) . We orient the direction \( {s}_{{N}^{\prime }} \) so that the positive direction points away from the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . The first step in proving this claim is to establish the following.

CLAIM A.24. Suppose that there is a two-sphere \( \sum  \subset  {N}^{\prime } \) contained in the closure of the positive half of \( {N}^{\prime } \) and also contained in \( \widetilde{C} \) . Suppose that \( \sum \) is isotopic in \( {N}^{\prime } \) to the central two-sphere \( {S}^{\prime } \) of \( {N}^{\prime } \) . Then \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) , a component containing \( X \) .

Proof. \( \sum \) separates \( \widetilde{C} \) into two components: \( A \) , which has compact closure in \( \widetilde{C} \) , and \( B \) , containing the end of \( \widetilde{C} \) . The two-sphere \( \sum \) also divides \( {C}^{\prime } \) into two components. Since \( \sum \) is isotopic in \( {N}^{\prime } \) to \( {S}^{\prime } \) , the complementary component \( {A}^{\prime } \) of \( \sum \) in \( {C}^{\prime } \) with compact closure contains the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . Of course, the frontier of \( A \) in \( M \) and the frontier of \( {A}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) are both equal to \( \sum \) . If \( A = {A}^{\prime } \) , then the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) is contained in the closure of \( A \) and hence is contained in \( \widetilde{C} \) , contradicting our assumption that \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) . Thus, \( A \) and \( {A}^{\prime } \) lie on opposite sides of their common frontier. This means that \( \bar{A} \cup  {\bar{A}}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) . Clearly, this component is also equal to \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) . Since \( X \) is connected and this component contains a point \( {x}_{0} \) of \( X \) , it contains \( X \) . This completes the proof of Claim A.24.

Now we return to the proof of Claim A.23. We consider three cases.

First Subcase: \( {S}^{\prime } \subset  \widetilde{C} \) . In this case we apply Claim A. 24 to see that \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) .

Second Subcase: \( {S}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from \( \widetilde{C} \) . Let \( A \) be the complementary component of \( {S}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) containing \( \widetilde{C} \) . The intersection of \( A \) with \( {C}^{\prime } \) is either the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) or is a submanifold of \( {C}^{\prime } \) diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . The first case is not possible since it would imply that the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains \( \widetilde{C} \) and hence contains \( {C}_{0} \) , contrary to the way we chose \( {C}_{0} \) . Thus, the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) and the complementary component \( A \) containing \( \widetilde{C} \) both have \( {S}^{\prime } \) as their frontier and they lie on opposite sides of \( {S}^{\prime } \) . Since the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) , it must be the case that \( {S}^{\prime } \) also contains a point of this frontier. By Proposition A.11, the neck \( {N}^{\prime } \subset  {C}^{\prime } \) meets \( {N}_{k} \) and there is a two-sphere \( \sum  \subset  {N}^{\prime } \cap  {N}_{k} \) isotopic in \( {N}^{\prime } \) to \( {S}^{\prime } \) and isotopic in \( {N}_{k} \) to the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{k} \) . Because \( {N}_{k} \subset  \widetilde{C} \) and \( \widetilde{C} \) is disjoint from the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) , we see that \( \sum \) is contained in the positive half of \( {N}^{\prime } \) . Applying Claim A. 24 we see that \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) .

Third Subcase: \( {S}^{\prime } \cap  \widetilde{C} \neq  \varnothing \) and \( {S}^{\prime } ⊄ \widetilde{C} \) . Clearly, in this case \( {S}^{\prime } \) contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) in \( M \) , i.e., a point of the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{k} \) in \( M \) . Since \( {N}_{k} \cap  {N}^{\prime } \neq  \varnothing \) , by Lemma A. 2 the scales of \( {N}_{k} \) and \( {N}^{\prime } \) are within \( 1 \pm  {0.01} \) of each other, and hence the diameter of \( {S}^{\prime } \) is at most \( {2\pi } \) times the scale of \( {N}_{k} \) . Since the central two-sphere \( {S}^{\prime } \) of \( {N}^{\prime } \) contains a point in the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{k} \) , it follows from Lemma A. 5 that \( {S}^{\prime } \) is contained on the positive side of the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{k} \) and that the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{k} \) is contained in \( {N}^{\prime } \) . By Proposition A. 11 there is a two-sphere \( \sum \) in the neck structure for \( {N}^{\prime } \) that is contained in \( {N}_{k} \) and is isotopic in \( {N}_{k} \) to the central two-sphere from that neck structure. Let \( A \) be the complementary component of \( \sum \) in \( M \) that contains \( \widetilde{C} \smallsetminus  {N}_{k} \) . If the complementary component of \( \sum \) that contains \( {C}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {N}^{\prime } \) is not \( A \) , then \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) . Suppose that \( A \) is also the complementary component of \( \sum \) in \( M \) that contains \( {C}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {N}^{\prime } \) . Of course, \( A \) is contained in the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . If \( k \geq  1 \) , we see that \( A \) and hence the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains \( \widetilde{C} \smallsetminus  {N}_{k} \) , which in turn contains the core of \( {C}_{0} \) . This contradicts our choice of \( {C}_{0} \) . If \( k = 0 \) , then \( {C}_{0} = A \cup  \left( {{N}_{0} \cap  \left( {M \smallsetminus  A}\right) }\right) \) . Of course, \( A \subset  {C}^{\prime } \) . Also, the frontier of \( {N}_{0} \cap  \left( {M \smallsetminus  A}\right) \) in \( M \) is the union of \( A \) and the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{0} \) in \( M \) . But we have already established that the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{0} \) in \( M \) is contained in \( {N}^{\prime } \) . Since \( A \subset  {C}^{\prime } \) , it follows that all of \( {C}_{0} \) is contained in \( {C}^{\prime } \) . On the other hand, there is a point of the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) contained in the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . This then contradicts our choice of \( {C}_{0} \) .

This completes the analysis of all the cases and hence completes the proof of Claim A.23.

The following holds for any \( \epsilon  < 1/4 \) and any \( C < \; \infty \) . Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a generalized Ricci flow and let \( x \in  \mathcal{M} \) be a point with \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  = t. \)

(1) Suppose that \( U \subset  {M}_{t} \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood for \( x \) . Then for any horizontal metric \( {G}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( {\left. G\right| }_{U} \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology, \( \left( {\left. U,{G}^{\prime }\right| }_{U}\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood for any \( {x}^{\prime } \in  U \) sufficiently close to \( x \) .

(2) Suppose that in \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) there is an evolving \( \epsilon \) -neck \( U \) centered at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) defined for an interval of normalized time of length \( a > 1 \) . Then any Ricci flow on

\[
U \times  \left( {t - {aR}{\left( x, t\right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack
\]

sufficiently close in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology to the pullback of \( G \) contains a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) .

(3) Given \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) and \( \left( {{C}^{\prime },{\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) \) with \( {C}^{\prime } > C \) and \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > \epsilon \) there is \( \delta  > 0 \) such that the following holds. Suppose that \( R\left( x\right)  \leq  2 \) . Let \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of \( x \) then for any metric \( {g}^{\prime } \) within \( \delta \) of \( g \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology \( \left( {U,{g}^{\prime }}\right) \) contains a \( \left( {{C}^{\prime },{\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) \) -neighborhood of \( x \) .

(4) Suppose that \( g\left( t\right) , - 1 < t \leq  0 \) , is a one-parameter family of metrics on \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) that is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( \left( {x,0}\right) \) and \( {R}_{g}\left( {x,0}\right)  = 1 \) . Then any one-parameter family \( {g}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) within \( \delta \) in the \( {C}^{\lbrack 1/\epsilon \rbrack } \) -topology of \( g \) with \( {R}_{{g}^{\prime }}\left( {x,0}\right)  = 1 \) is a strong \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) -neck.

Since \( \epsilon  < 1/4 \) , the diameter of \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) , the volume of \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) , the supremum over \( x \in  U \) of \( R\left( x\right) \) , the supremum over \( x \) and \( y \) in \( U \) of \( R\left( y\right) /R\left( x\right) \) , and the infimum over all 2-planes \( P \) in \( \mathcal{H}{TU} \) of \( K\left( P\right) \) are all continuous functions of the horizontal metric \( G \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology.

Let us consider the first statement. Suppose \( \left( {U,{\left. G\right| }_{U}}\right) \) is a \( C \) -component or an \( \epsilon \) -round component. Since the defining inequalities are strict, and, as we just remarked, the quantities in these inequalities vary continuously with the metric in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology, the result is clear in this case.

Let us consider the case when \( U \subset  {M}_{t} \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( x \) . Let \( \psi  : {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  U \) be the map giving the \( \epsilon \) -neck structure. Then for all horizontal metrics \( {G}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( G \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology, the same map \( \psi \) determines an \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( x \) for the structure \( \left( {\left. U,{G}^{\prime }\right| }_{U}\right) \) . Now let us consider moving \( x \) to a nearby point \( {x}^{\prime } \) , say \( {x}^{\prime } \) is the image of \( \left( {a, s}\right)  \in  {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . We pre-compose \( \psi \) by a map which is the product of the identity in the \( {S}^{2} \) -factor with a diffeomorphism \( \alpha \) on \( \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) that is the identity near the ends and moves 0 to \( s \) . As \( {x}^{\prime } \) approaches \( x, s \) tends to zero, and hence we can choose \( \alpha \) so that it tends to the identity in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology. Thus, for \( {x}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( x \) , this composition will determine an \( \epsilon \) -neck structure centered at \( {x}^{\prime } \) . Lastly, let us consider the case when \( \left( {U,{\left. G\right| }_{U}}\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core \( Y \) contains \( x \) . Let \( {G}^{\prime } \) be a horizontal metric sufficiently close to \( {\left. G\right| }_{U} \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology. Let \( N \subset  U \) be the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( U \smallsetminus  \bar{Y} \) . We have just seen that \( \left( {\left. N,{G}^{\prime }\right| }_{N}\right) \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck. Similarly, if \( {N}^{\prime } \subset  U \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck with central 2-sphere \( \partial \bar{Y} \) , then \( \left( {{N}^{\prime },{\left. {G}^{\prime }\right| }_{{N}^{\prime }}}\right) \) is an \( \epsilon \) -neck if \( {G}^{\prime } \) is sufficiently close to \( G \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology.

Thus, Conditions (1),(2), and (3) in the definition of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap hold for \( \left( {U,{G}_{U}^{\prime }}\right) \) . Since the curvature, volume and diameter inequalities in Conditions (4),(5), and (6) are strict, they also hold for \( {g}^{\prime } \) . To verify that Condition (7) holds for \( {G}^{\prime } \) , we need only remark that \( {r}_{y} \) is a continuous function of the metric. Lastly, since the derivative inequalities for the curvature in Condition (8) are strict inequalities and \( {\epsilon }^{-1} > 4 \) , if these inequalities hold for all horizontal metrics \( {G}^{\prime } \) sufficiently close to \( G \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology. This completes the examination of all cases and proves the first statement.

The second statement is proved in the same way using the fact that if \( {g}^{\prime }\left( t\right) \) is sufficiently close to \( g \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology and if \( {x}^{\prime } \) is sufficiently close to \( x \) , then \( {R}_{{g}^{\prime }}{\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} < a{R}_{g}{\left( x\right) }^{-1} \) .

Now let us turn to the third statement. The result is clear for \( \epsilon \) -necks. Also, since \( R\left( x\right)  \leq  2 \) the result is clear for \( \epsilon \) -round components and \( C \) - components as well. Lastly, we consider a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( U \) whose core \( Y \) contains \( x \) . Clearly, since \( R\left( x\right) \) is bounded above by 2, for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small, any metric \( {g}^{\prime } \) within \( \delta \) of \( g \) will satisfy the diameter, volume and curvature and the derivative of the curvature inequalities with \( {C}^{\prime } \) replacing \( C \) . Let \( N \) be the \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {U, g}\right) \) containing the end of \( U \) . Assuming that \( \delta \) is sufficiently small, let \( {N}^{\prime } \) be the image of \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},2{\left( {\epsilon }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} - {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . Then \( \left( {{N}^{\prime },{g}^{\prime }}\right) \) becomes an \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) -neck structure once we shift the parameter in the \( s \) -direction by \( {\epsilon }^{-1} - {\left( {\epsilon }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} \) . We let \( {U}^{\prime } = \bar{Y} \cup  {N}^{\prime } \) . Clearly, the \( \epsilon \) -neck with central 2-sphere \( \partial \bar{Y} \) will also determine an \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) -neck with the same central 2- sphere provided that \( \delta  > 0 \) is sufficiently small. Thus, for \( \delta  > 0 \) sufficiently small, for any \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) the result of this operation is a \( \left( {{C}^{\prime },{\epsilon }^{\prime }}\right) \) -cap with the same core.

The fourth statement is immediate.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]
