The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10A}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,\widehat{t},\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\widehat{t} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1},\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined.

Indeed, as in the first step of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, this follows directly from the gradient estimates (7.3.4) in the canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) .

Step 2. In this step, we will prove three time extension results.

Assertion 1. For arbitrarily fixed \( \alpha ,0 < A <  + \infty ,1 \leq  C <  + \infty \) and \( 0 \leq  B < \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{2}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1} \) , there is a \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) (independent of \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) with \( 0 \leq  b \leq  B \) and the scalar curvature satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C,\;\text{ on }{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack  ,
\]

then the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Before giving the proof, we make a simple observation: once a space point in the Ricci flow with surgery is removed by surgery at some time, then it never appears for later time; if a space point at some time \( t \) cannot be defined before the time \( t \) , then either the point lies in a gluing cap of the surgery at time \( t \) or the time \( t \) is the initial time of the Ricci flow.

Proof of Assertion 1. Firstly we claim that there exists \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) , the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined before the time \( - b \) (i.e., there are no surgeries interfering in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b - {\epsilon }^{\prime }, - b}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \left. {{\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0}\right) \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose not, then there is some point \( \widetilde{x} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) at \( \widetilde{x} \) cannot be defined before the time \( - b \) . By the above observation, there is a surgery at the time \( - b \) such that the point \( \widetilde{x} \) lies in the instant gluing cap.

Let \( \widetilde{h}\left( { = R{\left( \bar{x},\bar{t}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}h}\right) \) be the cut-off radius at the time \( - b \) for the rescaled solution. Clearly, there is a universal constant \( D \) such that \( {D}^{-1}\widetilde{h} \leq  \widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  D\widetilde{h} \) .

By Lemma 7.3.4 and looking at the rescaled solution at the time \( - b \) , the gluing cap and the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck, of radius \( \widetilde{h} \) , constitute a \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) . For any fixed small positive constant \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) (much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) ), we see that

\[
{\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  \mathcal{K}
\]

when \( \beta \) large enough. We first verify the following

CLAIM 1. For any small constants \( 0 < \widetilde{\theta } < 1,{\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) , there exists a \( \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right)  > 0 \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) , we have

(i) the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \)

(ii) the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) in the \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) evolved by the Ricci flow on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2} \) , \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\delta }^{\prime  - 1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the standard solution.

This claim essentially follows from Lemma 7.3.6. Indeed, suppose there is a surgery at some time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \in  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left( {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) which removes some point \( \widetilde{\widetilde{x}} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) . We assume \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \in  ( - b,0\rbrack \) is the first time with that property.

Then by Lemma 7.3.6, there is a \( \bar{\delta } = \bar{\delta }\left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) such that if \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } < \bar{\delta } \) , then the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) in the \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) evolved by the Ricci flow on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,\widetilde{\widetilde{t}}}\right) \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2},{\delta }^{\prime } \) -close to the corresponding subset of the standard solution. Note that the metrics for times in \( \lbrack  - b,\widetilde{\widetilde{t}}) \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) are equivalent. By Lemma 7.3.6, the solution on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) keeps looking like a cap for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-b,\widetilde{\widetilde{t}}}\right\rbrack \) . On the other hand, by the definition, the surgery is always done along the middle two-sphere of a \( \delta \) -neck with \( \delta  < {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) . Then for \( \beta \) large, all the points in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) are removed (as a part of a capped horn) at the time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \) . But \( \widetilde{x} \) (near the tip of the cap) exists past the time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \) . This is a contradiction. Hence we have proved that \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

The \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) -closeness of the solution on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}h}\right)  \times  \left( {\left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack  }\right) \) with the corresponding subset of the standard solution follows from Lemma 7.3.6. Then we have proved Claim 1.

We next verify the following

CLAIM 2. There is \( \widetilde{\theta } = \widetilde{\theta }\left( {CB}\right) ,0 < \widetilde{\theta } < 1 \) , such that \( b \leq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} \) when \( \beta \) large.

Note from Proposition 7.3.3, there is a universal constant \( {D}^{\prime } > 0 \) such that the standard solution satisfies the following curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {y, s}\right)  \geq  \frac{2{D}^{\prime }}{1 - s}.
\]

We choose \( \widetilde{\theta } = {D}^{\prime }/2\left( {{D}^{\prime } + {CB}}\right) \) . Then for \( \beta \) large enough, the rescaled solution satisfies

(7.4.15)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{1 - \left( {t + b}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{-2}}{\widetilde{h}}^{-2}
\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right)  \times  \left( {\left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack  }\right) \) .

Suppose \( b \geq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} \) . Then by combining with the assumption \( \widetilde{R}\left( {\widetilde{x}, t}\right)  \leq  C \) for \( t = \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} - b \) , we have

\[
C \geq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{1 - \left( {t + b}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{-2}}{\widetilde{h}}^{-2},
\]

and then

\[
1 \geq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) \left( {1 + \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{CB}}\right) .
\]

This is a contradiction. Hence we have proved Claim 2.

The combination of the above two claims shows that there is a positive constant \( 0 < \widetilde{\theta } = \widetilde{\theta }\left( {CB}\right)  < 1 \) such that for any small \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) , there is a positive \( \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) , we have \( b \leq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} \) and the rescaled solution in the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2},{\delta }^{\prime } \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the standard solution.

By (7.4.15) and the assumption \( \widetilde{R} \leq  C \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) , we know that the cut-off radius \( \widetilde{h} \) at the time \( - b \) for the rescaled solution satisfies

\[
\widetilde{h} \geq  \sqrt{\frac{{D}^{\prime }}{C}}.
\]

Let \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) be much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) and \( \min \left\{  {{A}^{-1}, A}\right\} \) . Since \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {\widetilde{x},\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  A \) , it follows that there is constant \( C\left( \widetilde{\theta }\right) \) depending only on \( \widetilde{\theta } \) such that \( {\widetilde{d}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  C\left( \widetilde{\theta }\right) A \ll \; {\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h} \) . We now apply Lemma 7.3.5 with the accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon /2 \) . Let \( C\left( {\varepsilon /2}\right) \) be the positive constant in Lemma 7.3.5. Without loss of generality, we may assume the positive constant \( {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) in the canonical neighborhood assumption is larger than \( {4C}\left( {\varepsilon /2}\right) \) . When \( {\delta }^{\prime }\left( { > 0}\right) \) is much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) and \( \min \left\{  {{A}^{-1}, A}\right\} \) , the point \( \bar{x} \) at the time \( \bar{t} \) has a neighborhood which is either a \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -cap or a \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck.

Since the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , the neighborhood of the point \( \bar{x} \) at the new time zero for the rescaled solution must be a \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck. By Lemma 7.3.5 (b), we know the neighborhood is the slice at the time zero of the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {\bar{x},0,\frac{4}{3}{\varepsilon }^{-1}\widetilde{R}{\left( \bar{x},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \min \left\{  {\widetilde{R}{\left( \bar{x},0\right) }^{-1}, b}\right\}  }\right)
\]

(with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {\bar{x},0}\right)  = 1 \) ) which is \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  \frac{4}{3}{\varepsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the evolving standard cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-\min \{ b,1\} ,0}\right\rbrack \) with scalar curvature 1 at the time zero. If \( b \geq  1 \) , the \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck is strong, which is a contradiction. While if \( b < 1 \) , the \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck at time \( - b \) is contained in the union of the gluing cap and the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck where the \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery took place. Since \( \varepsilon \) is small (say \( \varepsilon  < 1/{100} \) ), it is clear that the point \( \bar{x} \) at time \( - b \) is the center of an \( \varepsilon \) -neck which is entirely contained in the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck. By the proof of Lemma 7.3.2, the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck approximates an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. This implies the point \( \bar{x} \) at the time \( \bar{t} \) has a strong \( \varepsilon \) -neck, which is also a contradiction.

Hence we have proved that there exists \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) , the rescaled solution on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined before the time \( - b \) .

Let \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{A}^{\alpha \beta },0}\right\rbrack   \supset  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) be the largest time interval so that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) can be defined on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{A}^{\alpha \beta },0}\right\rbrack \) . We finally claim that \( {t}_{A}^{\alpha \beta } \leq   - b - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1} \) for \( \beta \) large enough.

Indeed, suppose not, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have the curvature estimate

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}
\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{A}^{\alpha \beta }, - b}\right\rbrack \) . Hence we have the curvature estimate

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}

We need to show \( - {t}_{\max } =  - \infty \) . Suppose \( - {t}_{\max } >  - \infty \) , there are only the following two possibilities: either

(1) The curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow   - {t}_{\max } \) ; or

(2) For each small constant \( \theta  > 0 \) and each large integer \( {k}_{0} > 0 \) , there is some \( k \geq \; {k}_{0} \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) has a surgery time \( {T}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \theta ,0}\right\rbrack \) and a surgery point \( {x}_{k} \) lying in a gluing cap at the times \( {T}_{k} \) so that \( {d}_{{T}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},\bar{x}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded from above by a constant independent of \( \theta \) and \( {k}_{0} \) .

We next claim that the possibility (1) always occurs. Suppose not; then the curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is bounded on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) by some positive constant \( \widehat{C} \) . In particular, for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a sufficiently large integer \( {k}_{1} > 0 \) such that any rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( k \geq  {k}_{1} \) on the geodesic ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and its scalar curvature is bounded by \( 2\widehat{C} \) there. (Here, without loss of generality, we may assume that the upper bound \( \widehat{C} \) is so large that \( - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1} < 0 \) .) By Assertion 1 in Step 2, for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and has the scalar curvature \( \widetilde{R} \leq  {10}\widehat{C} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . So we can extract a smooth limit from the sequence to get the limiting solution which is defined on a larger time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . This contradicts the definition of the maximal time \( - {t}_{\max } \) .

It remains to exclude the possibility (1).

By using Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5) again, we have

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}.
\]

So we only need to control the curvature near \( - {t}_{\max } \) . Exactly as in Step 4 in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, it follows from Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality that

(7.4.16)

\[
{\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {30}{t}_{\max }\sqrt{\widetilde{Q}}
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Since the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time, we have some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( - {t}_{\max } < {t}_{\infty } <  - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \; 5/4 \) . By (7.4.16), there is a constant \( {\widetilde{A}}_{0} > 0 \) such that \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{\infty }}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}/2 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Now we come back to the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) . Clearly, for arbitrarily given small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , when \( k \) large enough, there is a point \( {y}_{k} \) in the underlying manifold of \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at time 0 satisfying the following properties

(7.4.17)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \frac{3}{2},\;{\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By the definition of convergence, we know that for any fixed \( {A}_{0} \geq  2{\widetilde{A}}_{0} \) , for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{2{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}
\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) . Then by Assertion 2 of Step 2, we have proved that there is a sufficiently large integer \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) such that when \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at \( {y}_{k} \) can be defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {15}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) .

We now prove a statement analogous to Assertion 4 (i) of Step 3.

Assertion 5. For the above rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) and \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , we have that for any \( L > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \omega \left( L\right) \) such that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \omega \left( L\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  L \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) , and for all \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) .

Proof of Assertion 5. We slightly modify the argument in the proof of Assertion 4 (i). Let

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  \rho }\right. \text{ and }t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\text{ in the rescaled solutions }\left. {{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}, k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  > 0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Note that the estimate (7.4.14) implies that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . We only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose \( {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) . Then, after passing to a subsequence, there is a sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( {t}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\widetilde{d}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\widetilde{y}}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{k} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {\widetilde{y}}_{k} \) at the time \( {t}_{k} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic ball centered at \( {y}_{k} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

For any \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , by applying Assertion 3 as before, we get that the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho }\right) \) are defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) . By Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we further know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded. Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

(Hamilton [65]). Let \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) , be a noncollapsing nonsingular solution of the normalized Ricci flow on a compact three-manifold \( M \) . Then either

(i) there exist a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) and a sequence of diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{k} : M \rightarrow  M \) so that the pull-back of the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {t}_{k}\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{k} \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) topology to a metric on \( M \) with constant sectional curvature; or

(ii) we can find a finite collection of complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifolds \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) with finite volume, and for all \( t \) beyond some time \( T <  + \infty \) we can find compact subsets \( {K}_{1},\ldots ,{K}_{m} \) of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{1},\ldots ,{\mathcal{H}}_{m} \) respectively obtained by truncating each cusp of the hyperbolic manifolds along constant mean curvature torus of small area, and diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) ,1 \leq  l \leq  m \) , of \( {K}_{l} \) into \( M \) so that as long as \( t \) sufficiently large, the pull-back of the solution metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) by \( {\varphi }_{l}\left( t\right) \) is as close as to the hyperbolic metric as we like on the compact sets \( {K}_{1},\ldots ,{K}_{m} \) ; and moreover if we call the exceptional part of \( M \) those points where they are not in the image of any \( {\varphi }_{l} \) , we can take the injectivity radii of the exceptional part at everywhere as small as we like and the boundary tori of each \( {K}_{l} \) are incompressible in the sense that each \( {\varphi }_{l} \) injects \( {\pi }_{1}\left( {\partial {K}_{l}}\right) \) into \( {\pi }_{1}\left( M\right) \) .

The rest of this section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 5.3.4. We will divide the proof into three parts.

## Part I: Subsequence Convergence

According to Lemma 5.1.1, the scalar curvature of the normalized flow evolves by the equation

(5.3.3)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| Ric\right| }^{2} - \frac{2}{3}{rR}
\]

\[
= {\Delta R} + 2\left| \mathop{\operatorname{Ric}}\limits^{ \circ  }\right|  + \frac{2}{3}R\left( {R - r}\right)
\]

where \( \overset{ \circ  }{Ric} \) is the traceless part of the Ricci tensor. As before, we denote by \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = \; \mathop{\min }\limits_{{x \in  M}}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) . It then follows from the maximum principle that

(5.3.4)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{R}_{\min } \geq  \frac{2}{3}{R}_{\min }\left( {{R}_{\min } - r}\right) ,
\]

which implies that if \( {R}_{\min } \leq  0 \) it must be nondecreasing, and if \( {R}_{\min } \geq  0 \) it cannot go negative again. We can then divide the noncollapsing solutions of the normalized Ricci flow into three cases.

Case (1): \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  > 0 \) for some \( t > 0 \) ; Case (2): \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   + \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) ; Case (3): \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all \( t \in  \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   + \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  < 0 \) .

Let us first consider Case (1). In this case the maximal time interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) of the corresponding solution of the unnormalized flow is finite, since the unnormalized scalar curvature \( \widetilde{R} \) satisfies

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\widetilde{R} = \Delta \widetilde{R} + 2{\left| \widetilde{R}ic\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\geq  \Delta \widetilde{R} + \frac{2}{3}{\widetilde{R}}^{2}
\]

which implies that the curvature of the unnormalized solution blows up in finite time. Without loss of generality, we may assume that for the initial metric at \( t = 0 \) , the eigenvalues \( \widetilde{\lambda } \geq  \widetilde{\mu } \geq  \widetilde{\nu } \) of the curvature operator are bounded below by \( \widetilde{\nu } \geq   - 1 \) . It follows from Theorem 5.3.2 that the pinching estimate

\[
\widetilde{R} \geq  \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right\rbrack
\]

holds whenever \( \widetilde{\nu } < 0 \) . This shows that when the unnormalized curvature big, the negative ones are not nearly as large as the positive ones. Note that the unnormalized curvature becomes unbounded in finite time. Thus when we rescale the unnormalized flow to the normalized flow, the scaling factor must go to infinity. In the nonsingular case the rescaled positive curvature stay finite, so the rescaled negative curvature (if any) go to zero. Hence we can take a noncollapsing limit for the nonsingular solution of the normalized flow so that it has nonnegative sectional curvature.

Since the volume of the limit is finite, it follows from a result of Calabi and Yau [112] that the limit must be compact and the limiting manifold is the original one. Then by the strong maximum principle as in the proof of Theorem 5.2.3 (i), either the limit is flat, or it is a compact metric quotient of the product of a positively curved surface \( {\sum }^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) , or it has strictly positive curvature. By the work of Schoen-Yau [110], a flat three-manifold cannot have a metric of positive scalar curvature, but our manifold does in Case (1). This rules out the possibility of a flat limit. Clearly the limit is also a nonsingular solution to the normalized Ricci flow. Note that the curvature of the surface \( {\sum }^{2} \) has a positive lower bound and is compact since it comes from the lifting of the compact limiting manifold. From Theorem 5.1.11, we see the metric of the two-dimensional factor \( {\sum }^{2} \) converges to the round two-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) in the normalized Ricci flow. Note also that the normalized factors in two-dimension and three-dimension are different. This implies that the compact quotient of the product \( {\sum }^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) cannot be nonsingular, which is also ruled out for the limit. Thus the limit must have strictly positive sectional curvature. Since the convergence takes place everywhere for the compact limit, it follows that as \( t \) large enough the original nonsingular solution has strictly positive sectional curvature. This in turn shows that the corresponding unnormalized flow has strictly positive sectional curvature after some finite time. Then in views of the proof of Theorem 5.2.1, in particular the pinching estimate in Proposition 5.2.5, the limit has constant Ricci curvature and then constant sectional curvature for three-manifolds. This finishes the proof in Case (1).

We next consider Case (2). In this case we only need to show that we can take a noncollapsing limit which has nonnegative sectional curvature. Indeed, if this is true, then as in the previous case, the limit is compact and either it is flat, or it splits as a product (or a quotient of a product) of a positively curved \( {S}^{2} \) with a circle \( {S}^{1} \) , or it has strictly positive curvature. But the assumption \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq  0 \) for all times \( t \geq  0 \) in this case implies the limit must be flat.

Let us consider the corresponding unnormalized flow \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) associated to the non-collapsing nonsingular solution. The pinching estimate in Theorem 5.3.2 tells us that we may assume the unnormalized flow \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) exists for all times \( 0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) , for otherwise, the scaling factor approaches infinity as in the previous case which implies the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature. The volume \( \widetilde{V}\left( t\right) \) of the unnormalized solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) now changes. We divide the discussion into three subcases.

Subcase (2.1): there is a sequence of times \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) ;

Subcase (2.2): there is a sequence of times \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) ;

Subcase (2.3): there exist two positive constants \( {C}_{1},{C}_{2} \) such that \( {C}_{1} \leq  \widetilde{V}\left( t\right)  \leq  {C}_{2} \) for all \( 0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) .

For Subcase (2.1), because

\[
\frac{d\widetilde{V}}{dt} =  - r\widetilde{V}
\]

we have

\[
\log \frac{\widetilde{V}\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right) }{\widetilde{V}\left( 0\right) } =  - {\int }_{0}^{{\widetilde{t}}_{k}}r\left( t\right) {dt} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

which implies that there exists another sequence of times, still denoted by \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \) , such that \( {\widetilde{t}}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) and \( r\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{k}\right)  \leq  0 \) . Let \( {t}_{k} \) be the corresponding times for the normalized flow. Thus there holds for the normalized flow

\[
r\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0,\;\text{ as }\;k \rightarrow  \infty ,
\]

since \( 0 \geq  r\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \geq  {R}_{\min }\left( {t}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0 \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Then

\[
{\int }_{M}\left( {R - {R}_{\min }}\right) {d\mu }\left( {t}_{k}\right)  = \left( {r\left( {t}_{k}\right)  - {R}_{\min }\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) V \rightarrow  0,\;\text{ as }k \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

As we take a noncollapsing limit along the time sequence \( {t}_{k} \) , we get

\[
{\int }_{{M}^{\infty }}{Rd}{\mu }^{\infty } = 0
\]

for the limit of the normalized solutions at the new time \( t = 0 \) . But \( R \geq  0 \) for the limit because \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow   + \infty }}{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) for the nonsingular solution. So \( R = 0 \) at \( t = 0 \) for the limit. Since the limit flow exists for \( - \infty  < t <  + \infty \) and the scalar curvature of the limit flow evolves by

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}R = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\right| }^{2} - \frac{2}{3}{r}^{\infty }R,\;t \in  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right)
\]

where \( {r}^{\infty } \) is the limit of the function \( r\left( t\right) \) by translating the times \( {t}_{k} \) as the new time \( t = 0 \) . It follows from the strong maximum principle that

\[
R \equiv  0,\;\text{ on }\;{M}^{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) .
\]

This in turn implies, in view of the above evolution equation, that

\[
\operatorname{Ric} \equiv  0,\;\text{ on }\;{M}^{\infty } \times  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) .
\]

Hence this limit must be flat. Since the limit \( {M}^{\infty } \) is complete and has finite volume, the flat manifold \( {M}^{\infty } \) must be compact. Thus the underlying manifold \( {M}^{\infty } \) must agree with the original \( M \) (as a topological manifold). This says that the limit was taken on \( M \) .

For Subcase (2.2), we may assume as before that for the initial metric at \( t = 0 \) of the unnormalized flow \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) , the eigenvalues \( \widetilde{\lambda } \geq  \widetilde{\mu } \geq  \widetilde{\nu } \) of the curvature operator satisfy \( \widetilde{\nu } \geq   - 1 \) . It then follows from Theorem 5.3.2 that

\[
\widetilde{R} \geq  \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right) \left\lbrack  {\log \left( {-\widetilde{\nu }}\right)  + \log \left( {1 + t}\right)  - 3}\right\rbrack  ,\;\text{ for all }t \geq  0

## Part II: Persistence of Hyperbolic Pieces

We begin with the definition of the topology of \( {C}^{\infty } \) convergence on compact sets for maps \( F : M \rightarrow  N \) of one Riemannian manifold to another. For any compact set \( K \subset   \subset  M \) and any two maps \( F, G : M \rightarrow  N \) , we define

\[
{d}_{K}\left( {F, G}\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  K}}d\left( {F\left( x\right) , G\left( x\right) }\right)
\]

where \( d\left( {y, z}\right) \) is the geodesic distance from \( y \) to \( z \) on \( N \) . This gives the \( {C}_{loc}^{0} \) topology for maps between \( M \) and \( N \) . To define \( {C}_{loc}^{k} \) topology for any positive integer \( k \geq  1 \) , we consider the \( k \) -jet space \( {J}^{k}M \) of a manifold \( M \) which is the collection of all

\[
\left( {x,{J}^{1},{J}^{2},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right)
\]

where \( x \) is a point on \( M \) and \( {J}^{i} \) is a tangent vector for \( 1 \leq  i \leq  k \) defined by the \( {i}^{th} \) covariant derivative \( {J}^{i} = {\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{i}\gamma \left( 0\right) \) for a path \( \gamma \) passing through the point \( x \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x \) . A smooth map \( F : M \rightarrow  N \) induces a map

\[
{J}^{k}F : \;{J}^{k}M \rightarrow  {J}^{k}N
\]

defined by

\[
{J}^{k}F\left( {x,{J}^{1},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right)  = \left( {F\left( x\right) ,{\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}\left( {F\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \left( 0\right) ,\ldots ,{\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{k}\left( {F\left( \gamma \right) }\right) \left( 0\right) }\right)
\]

where \( \gamma \) is a path passing through the point \( x \) with \( {J}^{i} = {\nabla }_{\frac{\partial }{\partial t}}^{i}\gamma \left( 0\right) ,1 \leq  i \leq  k \) .

Define the k-jet distance between \( F \) and \( G \) on a compact set \( K \subset   \subset  M \) by

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( K\right) }\left( {F, G}\right)  = {d}_{B{J}^{k}K}\left( {{J}^{k}F,{J}^{k}G}\right)
\]

where \( B{J}^{k}K \) consists of all \( k \) -jets \( \left( {x,{J}^{1},\ldots ,{J}^{k}}\right) \) with \( x \in  K \) and

\[
{\left| {J}^{1}\right| }^{2} + {\left| {J}^{2}\right| }^{2} + \cdots  + {\left| {J}^{k}\right| }^{2} \leq  1
\]

Then the convergence in the metric \( {d}_{{C}^{k}\left( K\right) } \) for all positive integers \( k \) and all compact sets \( K \) defines the topology of \( {C}^{\infty } \) convergence on compact sets for the space of maps.

We will need the following Mostow type rigidity result.

LEMMA 5.3.7. For any complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifold \( \mathcal{H} \) with finite volume with metric \( h \) , we can find a compact set \( \mathcal{K} \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) such that for every integer \( k \) and every \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist an integer \( q \) and a \( \delta  > 0 \) with the following property: if \( F \) is a diffeomorphism of \( \mathcal{K} \) into another complete noncompact hyperbolic three-manifold \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) with no fewer cusps (than \( \mathcal{H} \) ), finite volume with metric \( \widetilde{h} \) such that

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}^{ * }\widetilde{h} - h\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{q}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) } < \delta
\]

then there exists an isometry I of \( \mathcal{H} \) to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) such that

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) }\left( {F, I}\right)  < \varepsilon .
\]

Proof. First we claim that \( \mathcal{H} \) is isometric to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) for an appropriate choice of compact set \( \mathcal{K} \) , positive integer \( q \) and positive number \( \delta \) . Let \( l : \mathcal{H} \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be a function defined at each point by the length of the shortest non-contractible loop starting and ending at this point. Denote the Margulis constant by \( \mu \) . Then by Margulis lemma (see for example [55] or [76]), for any \( 0 < {\varepsilon }_{0} < \frac{1}{2}\mu \) , the set \( {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  \mathcal{H} \) consists of finitely many components and each of these components is isometric to a cusp or to a tube. Topologically, a tube is just a solid torus. Let \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) be even smaller than one half of the minimum of the lengths of the all closed geodesics on the tubes. Then \( {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{\varepsilon }_{0}}\right\rbrack  \right) \) consists of finite number of cusps. Set \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} = {l}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{\varepsilon }_{0},\infty }\right) \right) \) . The boundary of \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) consists of flat tori with constant mean curvatures. Note that each embedded torus in a complete hyperbolic three-manifold with finite volume either bounds a solid torus or is isotopic to a standard torus in a cusp. The diffeomorphism \( F \) implies the boundary \( F\left( {\partial {\mathcal{K}}_{0}}\right) \) are embedded tori. If one of components bounds a solid torus, then as \( \delta \) sufficiently small and \( q \) sufficiently large, \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) would have fewer cusps than \( \mathcal{H} \) , which contradicts with our assumption. Consequently, \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) is diffeomorphic to \( F\left( {\mathcal{K}}_{0}\right) \) . Here \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) is the interior of the set \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) . Since \( \mathcal{H} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathcal{K}}_{0},\mathcal{H} \) is diffeomorphic to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) . Hence by Mostow’s rigidity theorem (see [97] and [107]), \( \mathcal{H} \) is isometric to \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} \) .

So we can assume \( \widetilde{\mathcal{H}} = \mathcal{H} \) . For \( \mathcal{K} = {\mathcal{K}}_{0} \) , we argue by contradiction. Suppose there is some \( k > 0 \) and \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) so that there exist sequences of integers \( {q}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty ,{\delta }_{j} \rightarrow  {0}^{ + } \) and diffeomorphisms \( {F}_{j} \) mapping \( \mathcal{K} \) into \( \mathcal{H} \) with

\[
{\begin{Vmatrix}{F}_{j}^{ * }h - h\end{Vmatrix}}_{{C}^{{q}_{j}}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) } < {\delta }_{j}
\]

and

\[
{d}_{{C}^{k}\left( \mathcal{K}\right) }\left( {{F}_{j}, I}\right)  \geq  \varepsilon
\]

for all isometries \( I \) of \( \mathcal{H} \) to itself. We can extract a subsequence of \( {F}_{j} \) convergent to a map \( {F}_{\infty } \) with \( {F}_{\infty }^{ * }h = h \) on \( \mathcal{K} \) .

We need to check that \( {F}_{\infty } \) is still a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . Since \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a local diffeomorphism and is the limit of diffeomorphisms, we can find an inverse of \( {F}_{\infty } \) on \( {F}_{\infty }\left( \mathcal{K}\right) \) . So \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . We claim the image of the boundary can not touch the image of the interior. Indeed, if \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{1}\right)  = {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{2}\right) \) with \( {x}_{1} \in  \partial \mathcal{K} \) and \( {x}_{2} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) , then we can find \( {x}_{3} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) near \( {x}_{1} \) and \( {x}_{4} \in  \overset{o}{\mathcal{K}} \) near \( {x}_{2} \) with \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{3}\right)  = {F}_{\infty }\left( {x}_{4}\right) \) , since \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a local diffeomorphism. This contradicts with the fact that \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) . This proves our claim. Hence, the only possible overlap is at the boundary. But the image \( {F}_{\infty }\left( {\partial \mathcal{K}}\right) \) is strictly concave, this prevents the boundary from touching itself. We conclude that the mapping \( {F}_{\infty } \) is a diffeomorphism on \( \mathcal{K} \) , hence an isometry.

To extend \( {F}_{\infty } \) to a global isometry, we argue as follows. For each truncated cusp end of \( \mathcal{K} \) , the area of constant mean curvature flat torus is strictly decreasing. Since \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes each such torus to another of the same area, we see that \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes the foliation of an end by constant mean curvature flat tori to another such foliation. So \( {F}_{\infty } \) takes cusps to cusps and preserves their foliations. Note that the isometric type of a cusp is just the isometric type of the torus, more precisely, let \( \left( {N, d{r}^{2} + {e}^{-{2r}}{g}_{\mathcal{V}}}\right) \) be a cusp (where \( {g}_{\mathcal{V}} \) is the flat metric on the torus \( \mathcal{V} \) ), \( 0 < a < b \) are two constants, any isometry of \( N \cap  {l}^{-1}\left\lbrack  {a, b}\right\rbrack \) to itself is just an isometry of \( \mathcal{V} \) . Hence the isometry \( {F}_{\infty } \) can be extended to the whole cusps. This gives a global isometry \( I \) contradicting our assumption when \( j \) large enough.

The proof of the Lemma 5.3.7 is completed. [
