this process must terminate after a finite number of steps and the last element fits.

Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) be the rescaled solutions obtained by rescaling \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) around \( {x}_{k} \) with the factors \( {Q}_{k} = {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and shifting the time \( {t}_{k} \) to the new time zero. Denote by \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k} \) the rescaled scalar curvature. We will show that a subsequence of the orientable rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which is a contradiction. In the following we divide the argument into four steps.

Step 1. First of all, we need a local bound on curvatures.

Lemma 7.1.2. For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\bar{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {d}_{\bar{t}}^{2}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \) , where \( {\bar{Q}}_{k} = {Q}_{k} + {R}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and \( c > 0 \) is a small universal constant.

Proof. Consider any point \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{\left( c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with \( c > 0 \) to be determined. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) , there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a space-time curve \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) that goes straight from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) and goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic (with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,\bar{t}}\right) \) ). If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with the scalar curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( {y}_{0} \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( {y}_{0} = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . On the segment of \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( {y}_{0} \) , the scalar curvature is at least \( 2{Q}_{k} \) . According to the choice of the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , the solution along the segment is \( \varepsilon \) -close to that of some ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. It follows from Theorem 6.4.3 (ii) that

\[
\left| {\nabla \left( {R}_{k}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2\eta }\text{ and }\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {R}_{k}^{-1}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2\eta }
\]

on the segment. (Here, without loss of generality, we may assume \( \varepsilon \) is suitably small). Then by choosing \( c > 0 \) (depending only on \( \eta \) ) small enough we get the desired curvature bound by integrating the above derivative estimates along the segment. This proves the lemma.

Step 2. Next we want to show that for each \( A <  + \infty \) , there exist a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) (independent of \( k \) ) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions

\( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the new time \( t = 0 \) (corresponding to the original times \( {t}_{k} \) ) satisfy the estimate

\[
\left| \widetilde{R{m}_{k}}\right| \left( {y,0}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

whenever \( {d}_{{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\left( {y,{x}_{k}}\right)  \leq  A \) and \( k \geq  1 \) .

For each \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , set

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \mid  k \geq  1, x \in  {M}_{k}\text{ with }{d}_{0}\left( {x,{x}_{k}}\right)  \leq  \rho }\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

By the pinching estimate (7.1.1), it suffices to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) .

Note that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) by applying Lemma 7.1.2 with \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We now argue by contradiction to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) . Suppose not, we may find (after passing to a subsequence if necessary) a sequence of points \( {y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {d}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{y}_{k},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{k}\left( { \subset  {M}_{k}}\right) \) be a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \in  {\gamma }_{k} \) be the point on \( {\gamma }_{k} \) closest to \( {y}_{k} \) with \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right)  = 2 \) , and let \( {\beta }_{k} \) be the subsegment of \( {\gamma }_{k} \) running from \( {z}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . By Lemma 7.1.2 the length of \( {\beta }_{k} \) is bounded away from zero independent of \( k \) . By the pinching estimate (7.1.1), for each \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) , we have a uniform bound on the curvatures on the open balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}}\right) \) . The injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the time \( t = 0 \) are also uniformly bounded from below by the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property. Therefore by Lemma 7.1.2 and Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , the segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) , and \( {\beta }_{k} \) converges to a subsegment \( {\beta }_{\infty } \) of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . Let \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) denote the completion of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) .

Denote by \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty } \) the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since the rescaled scalar curvatures \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k} \) along \( {\beta }_{k} \) are at least 2, it follows from the choice of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) that for any \( {q}_{0} \in  {\beta }_{\infty } \) , the manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) in \( \left\{  {q \in  {B}_{\infty } \mid  {\operatorname{dist}}_{{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}^{2}\left( {q,{q}_{0}}\right)  < C\left( \varepsilon \right) {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-1}}\right\} \) is \( {2\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of (a time slice of) some orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Then by Theorem 6.4.6, we know that the orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution at each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has a radius \( r,0 < r < {C}_{1}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , such that its canonical neighborhood \( B \) , with \( {B}_{t}\left( {x, r}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{t}\left( {x,{2r}}\right) \) , is either an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, or an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, or a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) , and moreover the scalar curvature is between \( {\left( {C}_{2}\left( 2\varepsilon \right) \right) }^{-1}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) R\left( {x, t}\right) \) , where \( {C}_{1}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) \) are the positive constants in Theorem 6.4.6.

We now choose \( C\left( \varepsilon \right)  = \max \left\{  {2{C}_{1}^{2}\left( {2\varepsilon }\right) ,{\varepsilon }^{-2}}\right\} \) . By the local curvature estimate in Lemma 7.1.2, we see that the scalar curvature \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty } \) becomes unbounded when approaching \( {y}_{\infty } \) along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . This implies that the canonical neighborhood around \( {q}_{0} \) cannot be a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) . Note that \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) is shortest since it is the limit of a sequence of shortest geodesics. Without loss of generality, we may assume \( \varepsilon \) is suitably small (say, \( \varepsilon  \leq  \frac{1}{100} \) ). These imply that as \( {q}_{0} \) gets sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) , the canonical neighborhood around \( {q}_{0} \) cannot be an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Thus we conclude that each \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) is the center of an evolving \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck.

Let

\[
U = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}B\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \;\left( { \subset  \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }}\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( B\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) is the ball centered at \( {q}_{0} \in  {B}_{\infty } \) with the radius \( {4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Clearly \( U \) has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching estimate (7.1.1). Since the metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) , we see that the metric space \( \bar{U} = U \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) by adding in the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) , is locally complete and intrinsic near \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Furthermore \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{U} \) . This implies the curvature of \( \bar{U} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) is nonnegative in the Alexandrov sense. It is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 10.9.3 and Corollary 10.9.5 of [9]) that there exists a three-dimensional tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) which is a metric cone. It is clear that its aperture is \( \leq  {10\varepsilon } \) , thus the tangent cone is nonflat.

Pick a point \( p \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) such that the distance from the vertex \( {y}_{\infty } \) to \( p \) is one and it is nonflat around \( p \) . Then the ball \( B\left( {p,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) by some factors \( {a}_{k} \) , where \( {s}_{k} \rightarrow  {0}^{ + } \) . Since the tangent cone is three-dimensional and nonflat around \( p \) , the factors \( {a}_{k} \) must be comparable with \( {\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{p}_{k},0}\right) \) . By using the local curvature estimate in Lemma 7.1.2, we actually have the convergence in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology for the solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) on the balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{p}_{k},{s}_{k}}\right) \) and over some time interval \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-\delta ,0}\right\rbrack \) for some sufficiently small \( \delta  > 0 \) . The limiting ball \( B\left( {p,\frac{1}{2}}\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{U} \) is a piece of the nonnegative curved and nonflat metric cone whose radial directions are all Ricci flat. On the other hand, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle to the evolution equation of the Ricci curvature tensor as in the proof of Lemma 6.3.1, the limiting ball \( B\left( {p,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \) would split off all radial directions isometrically (and locally). Since the limit is nonflat around \( p \) , this is impossible. Therefore we have proved that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the new times \( t = 0 \) (corresponding to the original times \( {t}_{k} \) ) stay uniformly bounded at bounded distances from \( {x}_{k} \) for all \( k \) .

We have proved that for each \( A <  + \infty \) , the curvature of the marked manifold \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) at each point \( y \in  {M}_{k} \) with distance from \( {x}_{k} \) at most \( A \) is bounded by \( C\left( A\right) \) . Lemma 7.1.2 extends this curvature control to a backward parabolic neighborhood centered at \( y \) whose radius depends only on the distance from \( y \) to \( {x}_{k} \) . Thus by Shi's local derivative estimates (Theorem 1.4.2) we can control all derivatives of the curvature in such backward parabolic neighborhoods. Then by using the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) subsequent limit to obtain \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , which is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales and is defined on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing the time slice \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \{ 0\} \) . Clearly it follows from the pinching estimate (7.1.1) that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator (and hence nonnegative sectional curvature).

Step 3. We further claim that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) at the time slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) has bounded curvature.

We know that the sectional curvature of the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is nonnegative everywhere. Argue by contradiction. Suppose the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is not bounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, there exists a sequence of points \( {q}_{j} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) diverging to infinity such that their scalar curvatures \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( j \rightarrow   + \infty \)

and

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for \( x \in  B\left( {{q}_{j}, j/\sqrt{{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right) }}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) . By combining with Lemma 7.1.2 and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing, a subsequence of the rescaled and marked manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{j},0}\right) {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{q}_{j}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth nonflat limit \( Y \) . By Proposition 6.1.2, the new limit \( Y \) is isometric to a metric product \( N \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some two-dimensional manifold \( N \) . On the other hand, in view of the choice of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , the original limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) ,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) at the point \( {q}_{j} \) has a canonical neighborhood which is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, or a compact manifold (without boundary) diffeomorphic to a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) . It follows that for \( j \) large enough, \( {q}_{j} \) is the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck of radius \( {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{j},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . Without loss of generality, we may further assume that \( {2\varepsilon } < {\varepsilon }_{0} \) , where \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) is the positive constant given in Proposition 6.1.1. Since \( {\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{j},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \rightarrow  0 \) as \( j \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this contradicts Proposition 6.1.1. So the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot ,0}\right) }\right) \) is bounded.

Step 4. Finally we want to extend the limit backwards in time to \( - \infty \) .

By Lemma 7.1.2 again, we now know that the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( a > 0 \) .

Denote by

\( {t}^{\prime } = \inf \{ \widetilde{t} \mid \) we can take a smooth limit on \( (\widetilde{t},0\rbrack \) (with bounded curvature at each time slice) from a subsequence of the convergent rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) \}.

We first claim that there is a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Indeed, let \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \) be a sequence of negative numbers such that \( {t}_{k}^{\prime } \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) and there exist smooth limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) defined on \( \left( {{t}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . For each \( k \) , the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature and has bounded curvature at each time slice. Moreover by Lemma 7.1.2, the limit has bounded curvature on each subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left( {{t}_{k}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Denote by \( \widetilde{Q} \) the scalar curvature upper bound of the limit at time zero (where \( \widetilde{Q} \) is the same for all \( k \) ). Then we can apply the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.7) to get

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\left( \frac{-{t}_{k}^{\prime }}{t - {t}_{k}^{\prime }}\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {x, t}\right) \) are the scalar curvatures of the limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }^{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) . Hence by the definition of convergence and the above curvature estimates, we can find a subsequence of the above convergent rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{k} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) .

We next claim that \( {t}^{\prime } =  - \infty \) .

Suppose not, then by Lemma 7.1.2, the curvature of the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By applying the maximum principle to the evolution equation of the scalar curvature, we see that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Note that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1 \) . Thus there exists some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right)  < \frac{3}{2}
\]

where \( c > 0 \) is the universal constant in Lemma 7.1.2. By using Lemma 7.1.2 again we see that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) in a small neighborhood of the point \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right) \) extends backwards to the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{10},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . We remark that the distances at time \( t \) and time 0 are roughly equivalent in the following sense

(7.1.3)

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - \text{ const. }
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Indeed from the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.7) we have the estimate

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\left( \frac{-{t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}\right) ,\;\text{ on }{M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack  .
\]

By applying Lemma 3.4.1 (ii), we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {30}\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) \sqrt{\widetilde{Q}}
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . On the other hand, since the curvature of the limit metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is nonnegative, we have

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  {d}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Thus we obtain the estimate (7.1.3).

Let us still denote by \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) the subsequence which converges on the maximal time interval \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . Consider the rescaled sequence \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) with the marked points \( {x}_{k} \) replaced by the associated sequence of points \( {y}_{k} \rightarrow  {y}_{\infty } \) and the (original unshifted) times \( {t}_{k} \) replaced by any \( {s}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{20}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k} + \left( {{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{20}}\right) {Q}_{k}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . It follows from Lemma 7.1.2 that for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) at \( {y}_{k} \) satisfy

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {10}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{10},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . By applying the same arguments as in the above Step 2, we conclude that for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right)  <  + \infty \) such that

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  A \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{20},{t}^{\prime } + \frac{c}{20}}\right\rbrack \) . The estimate (7.1.3) implies that there is a positive constant \( {A}_{0} \) such that for arbitrarily given small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \in  \left( {0,\frac{c}{100}}\right) \) , for \( k \) large enough, there hold

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {A}_{0}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By combining with Lemma 7.1.2, we then conclude that for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \widetilde{C}\left( A\right) \) such that for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) satisfy

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{C}\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime } - \frac{c}{100}{\left( C\left( A\right) \right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the (original) rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) , we see that the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is defined on a spacetime open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By repeating the argument of Step 3 and using Lemma 7.1.2, we further conclude the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) has uniformly bounded curvature on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . This is a contradiction.

Therefore we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\widetilde{g}}_{k}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which gives the desired contradiction. This completes the proof of the theorem. 0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sigma-Invariant Classification of Closed Oriented 3-Manifolds
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( M \) be a closed connected oriented 3-manifold.

(a) If \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) then \( M \) is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of a finite number of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) . Conversely, each such manifold has \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) .

(b) \( M \) is a graph manifold if and only if \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \geq  0 \) .

(c) If \( \sigma \left( M\right)  < 0 \) then \( {\left( -\frac{2}{3}\sigma \left( M\right) \right) }^{\frac{3}{2}} \) is the minimum of the numbers \( V \) with the following property : M can be decomposed as a connected sum of a finite collection of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s, metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) and some other components, the union of which is denoted by \( {M}^{\prime } \) , and there exists a (possibly disconnected) complete finite-volume manifold \( N \) with constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) and volume \( V \) which can be embedded in \( {M}^{\prime } \) so that the complement \( {M}^{\prime } - N \) (if nonempty) is a graph manifold.

Moreover, if \( \operatorname{vol}\left( N\right)  = {\left( -\frac{2}{3}\sigma \left( M\right) \right) }^{\frac{3}{2}} \) then the cusps of \( N \) (if any) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
If \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) then \( M \) has a metric \( g \) of positive scalar curvature. From Lemmas 81.1 and \( {81.2}, M \) is a connected sum of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) . Conversely, if \( M \) is a connected sum of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) then \( M \) admits a metric \( g \) of positive scalar curvature and so \( \sigma \left( M\right)  > 0 \) .

Now suppose that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \leq  0 \) . If \( M \) is a graph manifold then \( M \) volume-collapses with bounded curvature, so (93.6) implies that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  = 0 \) .

Suppose that \( M \) is not a graph manifold. Suppose that we have a given decomposition of \( M \) as a connected sum of a finite collection of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s, metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) and some other components, the union of which is denoted by \( {M}^{\prime } \) , and there exists a (possibly disconnected) finite-volume complete manifold \( N \) with constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) which can be embedded in \( {M}^{\prime } \) so that the complement (if nonempty) is a graph manifold. Let \( {V}_{hyp} \) denote the hyperbolic volume of \( N \) . We do not assume that the cusps of \( N \) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) . For any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , we claim that there is a metric \( {g}_{\epsilon } \) on \( M \) with \( R \geq   - 6 \cdot  \frac{1}{4} - \epsilon \) and volume \( V\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right)  \leq  {V}_{\text{ hyp }} + \epsilon \) . This comes from collapsing the graph manifold pieces, along with the fact that the connected sum operation can be performed while decreasing the scalar curvature arbitrarily little and increasing the volume arbitrarily little. Then \( {R}_{\min }\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right) V{\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right) }^{\frac{2}{3}} \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}^{2/3} - \) const. \( \epsilon \) . Thus \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}^{2/3} \) .

Let \( \widehat{V} \) denote the minimum of \( {V}_{hyp} \) over all such decompositions of \( M \) . (As the set of volumes of complete finite-volume 3-manifolds with constant curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) is well-ordered, there is a minimum.) Then \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) .

Next, take an arbitrary metric \( {g}_{0} \) on \( M \) and consider the Ricci flow \( g\left( t\right) \) with initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) . From Sections 90 and 92, there is a nonempty manifold \( N \) with a complete finite-volume metric of constant curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) so that for large \( t \) , there is a decomposition \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } = \; {M}_{1}\left( t\right)  \cup  {M}_{2}\left( t\right) \) of the time- \( t \) manifold, where \( {M}_{1}\left( t\right) \) is a graph manifold and \( \left( {{M}_{2}\left( t\right) ,{\left. \frac{1}{t}g\left( t\right) \right| }_{{M}_{2}\left( t\right) }}\right) \) is close to a large piece of \( N \) . In terms of condition (c) of Proposition 93.9, we will think of \( {M}^{\prime } \) as being \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) . Because of the presence of \( N \) , we know that \( t{R}_{\min }\left( t\right)  \leq   - \frac{3}{2} + \epsilon \left( t\right) \) and \( V\left( t\right)  \geq  {t}^{2/3}{V}_{hyp}\left( N\right)  - \epsilon \left( t\right) \) for a function \( \epsilon \left( t\right) \) with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}\epsilon \left( t\right)  = 0 \) . The monotonicity of \( {R}_{\min }\left( t\right) {V}^{2/3}\left( t\right) \) , even through surgeries, implies that

(93.10)

\[
{R}_{\min }\left( {g}_{0}\right) {V}^{2/3}\left( {g}_{0}\right)  \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{\text{ hyp }}{\left( N\right) }^{2/3} \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3}.
\]

Thus \( \sigma \left( M\right)  \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) .

This shows that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  =  - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) . Now take a decomposition of \( M \) as in condition (c) of Proposition 93.9, with \( {V}_{hyp}\left( N\right)  = \widehat{V} \) . We claim that the cuspidal 2-tori of \( N \) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) . If not then there would be a metric \( g \) on \( M \) with \( R\left( g\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2} \) and \( \operatorname{vol}\left( g\right)  < {V}_{hyp}\left( N\right) \) [3, Pf. of Theorem 2.9]. This would contradict the fact that \( \sigma \left( M\right)  =  - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}{\left( N\right) }^{2/3}. \)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(cf. II.8.2) Let \( M \) be a closed connected oriented 3-manifold.

(a) If \( M \) admits a metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) then it is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of a finite number of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) . Conversely, each such manifold admits a metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) .

(b) Suppose that \( M \) does not admit any metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) . Let \( \bar{\lambda } \) denote the supremum of \( \lambda \left( g\right) V{\left( g\right) }^{\frac{2}{3}} \) over all metrics \( g \) on \( M \) . Then \( M \) is a graph manifold if and only if \( \bar{\lambda } = 0 \) . (c) Suppose that \( M \) does not admit any metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) , and \( \bar{\lambda } < 0 \) . Then \( {\left( -\frac{2}{3}\bar{\lambda }\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}} \) is the minimum of the numbers \( V \) with the following property : \( M \) can be decomposed as a connected sum of a finite collection of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s, metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) and some other components, the union of which is denoted by \( {M}^{\prime } \) , and there exists a (possibly disconnected) complete manifold \( N \) with constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) and volume \( V \) which can be embedded in \( {M}^{\prime } \) so that the complement \( {M}^{\prime } - N \) (if nonempty) is a graph manifold.

Moreover, if \( \operatorname{vol}\left( N\right)  = {\left( -\frac{2}{3}\bar{\lambda }\right) }^{\frac{3}{2}} \) then the cusps of \( N \) (if any) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We first give the argument for Proposition 93.11 under the pretense that all Ricci flows are smooth, except for possible extinction of components. (Of course this is not the case, but it will allow us to present the main idea of the proof.)

If \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) for some metric \( g \) then from (93.2), the Ricci flow starting from \( g \) will become extinct within time \( \frac{3}{{2\lambda }\left( g\right) } \) . Hence Lemma 81.2 applies. Conversely, if \( M \) is a connected sum of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s and metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) then \( M \) admits a metric \( g \) of positive scalar curvature. From (93.3), \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) .

Now suppose that \( M \) does not admit any metric \( g \) with \( \lambda \left( g\right)  > 0 \) . If \( M \) is a graph manifold then \( M \) volume-collapses with bounded curvature, so (93.3) implies that \( \bar{\lambda } = 0 \) .

Suppose that \( M \) is not a graph manifold. Suppose that we have a given decomposition of \( M \) as a connected sum of a finite collection of \( {S}^{1} \times  {S}^{2} \) ’s, metric quotients of the round \( {S}^{3} \) and some other components, the union of which is denoted by \( {M}^{\prime } \) , and there exists a (possibly disconnected) complete manifold \( N \) with constant sectional curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) which can be embedded in \( {M}^{\prime } \) so that the complement (if nonempty) is a graph manifold. Let \( {V}_{hyp} \) denote the hyperbolic volume of \( N \) . We do not assume that the cusps of \( N \) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) . For any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , we claim that there is a metric \( {g}_{\epsilon } \) on \( M \) with \( R \geq   - 6 \cdot  \frac{1}{4} - \epsilon \) and volume \( V\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right)  \leq  {V}_{hyp} + \epsilon \) . This comes from collapsing the graph manifold pieces, along with the fact that the connected sum operation can be performed while decreasing the scalar curvature arbitrarily little and increasing the volume arbitrarily little. Then (93.3) implies that \( \lambda \left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right) V{\left( {g}_{\epsilon }\right) }^{\frac{2}{3}} \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}^{2/3} \) - const. \( \epsilon \) . Thus \( \bar{\lambda } \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}^{2/3} \) .

Let \( \widehat{V} \) denote the minimum of \( {V}_{hyp} \) over all such decompositions of \( M \) . (As the set of volumes of complete finite-volume 3-manifolds with constant curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) is well-ordered, there is a minimum.) Then \( \bar{\lambda } \geq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) .

Next, take an arbitrary metric \( {g}_{0} \) on \( M \) and consider the Ricci flow \( g\left( t\right) \) with initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) . From Sections 90 and 92, there is a nonempty manifold \( N \) with a finite-volume complete metric of constant curvature \( - \frac{1}{4} \) so that for large \( t \) , there is a decomposition of the time- \( t \) manifold \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } = {M}_{1}\left( t\right)  \cup  {M}_{2}\left( t\right) \) where \( {M}_{1}\left( t\right) \) is a graph manifold and \( \left( {{M}_{2}\left( t\right) ,{\left. \frac{1}{t}g\left( t\right) \right| }_{{M}_{2}\left( t\right) }}\right) \) is close to a large piece of \( N \) . As \( N \) has finite volume, a constant function on \( N \) is square-integrable and so inf spec \( \left( {-{\bigtriangleup }_{N}}\right)  = 0 \) . Equivalently,

(93.12)

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{f \in  {C}_{c}^{\infty }\left( N\right) , f \neq  0}}\frac{{\int }_{N}{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}{\mathrm{{dvol}}}_{N}}{{\int }_{N}{f}^{2}{\mathrm{{dvol}}}_{N}} = 0.
\]

Taking an appropriate test function \( \Phi \) on \( M \) with compact support in \( {M}_{2}\left( t\right) \) gives \( {t\lambda }\left( t\right)  \leq \; - \frac{3}{2} + {\epsilon }_{1}\left( t\right) \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}{\epsilon }_{1}\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . In terms of condition (c) of Proposition 93.11, we will think of \( {M}^{\prime } \) as being \( {\mathcal{M}}_{t}^{ + } \) . From the presence of \( N \) , we know that \( V\left( t\right)  \geq  {t}^{2/3}{V}_{\text{ hyp }}\left( N\right)  - {\epsilon }_{2}\left( t\right) \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  \infty }}{\epsilon }_{2}\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . As we are assuming that the Ricci flow is nonsingular, the monotonicity of \( \lambda \left( t\right) {V}^{2/3}\left( t\right) \) implies that

(93.13)

\[
\lambda \left( {g}_{0}\right) {V}^{2/3}\left( {g}_{0}\right)  \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{\text{ hyp }}{\left( N\right) }^{2/3} \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3}.
\]

Thus \( \bar{\lambda } \leq   - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) .

This shows that \( \bar{\lambda } =  - \frac{3}{2}{\widehat{V}}^{2/3} \) . Now take a decomposition of \( M \) as in condition (c) of Proposition 93.11, with \( {V}_{hyp}\left( N\right)  = \widehat{V} \) . We claim that the cuspidal 2-tori of \( N \) are incompressible in \( {M}^{\prime } \) . If not then there would be a metric \( g \) on \( M \) with \( R\left( g\right)  \geq   - \frac{3}{2} \) and vol \( \left( g\right)  < {V}_{hyp}\left( N\right) \) [3, Pf. of Theorem 2.9]. Using (93.3), one would obtain a contradiction to the fact that \( \bar{\lambda } =  - \frac{3}{2}{V}_{hyp}{\left( N\right) }^{2/3} \) .

To handle the behaviour of \( \lambda \left( t\right) {V}^{\frac{2}{3}}\left( t\right) \) under Ricci flows with surgery, we first state a couple of general facts about Schrödinger operators.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose that \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) is a generalized Ricci flow satisfying Assumptions (1) - (7). Let \( t \) be a singular time. Then the following holds for any \( {t}^{ - } < t \) sufficiently close to \( t \) . The manifold \( {M}_{{t}^{ - }} \) is diffeomorphic to a manifold obtained in the following way. Take the disjoint union of \( {M}_{t} \) , finitely many 2-sphere bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) , and finitely many closed 3-manifolds admitting metrics of constant positive curvature. Then perform connected sum operations between (some subsets of) these components.

Fix \( {t}^{\prime } < t \) but sufficiently close to \( t \) . By Assumption (4) every component of \( {E}_{t} \) is a 3-ball and hence every component of \( \partial {E}_{t} = \partial {C}_{t} \) is a 2-sphere. Since \( {C}_{t} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {C}_{{t}^{\prime }} \subset  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) we see that every component of \( \partial {C}_{{t}^{\prime }} = \partial {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a 2-sphere. Since every component of \( {E}_{t} \) is a 3-ball, the passage from the smooth manifold \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) to the smooth manifold \( {M}_{t} \) is effected by removing the interior of \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) from \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and gluing a 3-ball onto each component of \( \partial {C}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) to form \( {M}_{t} \) .

By Assumption (5) every point of \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Since \( \epsilon \) is sufficiently small it follows from Proposition A. 25 that every component of \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) that is also a component of \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is diffeomorphic either to a manifold admitting a metric of constant positive curvature (a 3-dimensional space-form), to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or to a 2-sphere bundle over \( {S}^{1} \) . In the passage from \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) to \( {M}_{t} \) these components are removed.

Now let us consider a component of \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) that is not a component of \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Such a component is a connected subset of \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) with the property that every point is either contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck and whose frontier in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) consists of 2-spheres that are central 2-spheres of \( \epsilon \) -necks. If every point is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck, then according to Proposition A.19, \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is an \( \epsilon \) -tube and in particular is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) . Otherwise \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is contained in a capped or double capped \( \epsilon \) -tube. Since the frontier of \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is non-empty and is the union of central 2-spheres of an \( \epsilon \) -neck, it follows that either \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is diffeomorphic to a capped \( \epsilon \) -tube or to an \( \epsilon \) -tube. Hence, these components of \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) are diffeomorphic either to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) , to \( {D}^{3} \) , or to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \smallsetminus  {B}^{3} \) . Replacing a 3-ball component of \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) by another 3-ball leaves the topology unchanged. Replacing a component of \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) that is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) by the disjoint union of two 3-balls has the effect of doing a surgery along the core 2-sphere of the cylinder \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) in \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . If this 2-sphere separates \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) into two pieces then doing this surgery effects a connected sum decomposition. If this 2-sphere does not separate, then the surgery has the topological effect of doing a connected sum decomposition into two pieces, one of which is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \) , and then removing that component entirely. Replacing a component of \( {D}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) that

is diffeomorphic to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \smallsetminus  {B}^{3} \) by a 3-ball, has the effect of doing a connected sum decomposition on \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) into pieces, one of which is diffeomorphic to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) , and then removing that component.

From this description the proposition follows immediately.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( \left( {{M}_{0},{g}_{0}}\right) \) be a connected Riemannian manifold with no locally separating \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) . Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a Ricci flow with surgery defined for \( 0 \leq  t < \infty \) with \( \left( {{M}_{0},{g}_{0}}\right) \) as initial manifold. Then the following four conditions are equivalent:

(1) \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) becomes extinct after a finite time, i.e., \( {M}_{T} = \varnothing \) for all \( T \) sufficiently large,

(2) \( {M}_{0} \) is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of three-dimensional spherical space-forms and \( {S}^{2} \) -bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) ,

(3) the fundamental group of \( {M}_{0} \) is a free product of finite groups and infinite cyclic groups,

(4) no prime \( {}^{4} \) factor of \( {M}_{0} \) is acyclic, i.e., every prime factor of \( {M}_{0} \) has either non-trivial \( {\pi }_{2} \) or non-trivial \( {\pi }_{3} \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex: Repeated application of Theorem 0.3 shows that (1) implies (2). The implication (2) implies (3) is immediate from van Kampen's theorem. The fact that (3) implies (1) is Theorem 0.4. This shows that (1), (2) and (3) are all equivalent. Since three-dimensional spherical space-forms and \( {S}^{2} \) -bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) are easily seen to be prime,(2) implies (4). Thus, it remains only to see that (4) implies (3). We consider a manifold \( M \) satisfying (4), a prime factor \( P \) of \( M \) , and universal covering \( \widetilde{P} \) of \( P \) . First suppose that \( {\pi }_{2}\left( P\right)  = {\pi }_{2}\left( \widetilde{P}\right) \) is trivial. Then, by hypothesis \( {\pi }_{3}\left( P\right)  = {\pi }_{3}\left( \widetilde{P}\right) \) is non-trivial. By the Hurewicz theorem this means that \( {H}_{3}\left( \widetilde{P}\right) \) is non-trivial, and hence that \( \widetilde{P} \) is a compact, simply connected three-manifold. It follows that \( {\pi }_{1}\left( P\right) \) is finite. Now suppose that \( {\pi }_{2}\left( P\right) \) is non-trivial. Then \( P \) is not diffeomorphic to \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . Since \( P \) is prime and contains no locally separating \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) , it follows that \( P \) contains no embedded \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{2} \) . Then by the sphere theorem there is an embedded 2-sphere in \( P \) that is homotopically non-trivial. Since \( P \) is prime, this sphere cannot separate, so cutting \( P \) open along it produces a connected manifold \( {P}_{0} \) with two boundary 2-spheres. Since \( {P}_{0} \) is prime, it follows that \( {P}_{0} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) and hence \( P \) is diffeomorphic to a 2-sphere bundle over the circle.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Suppose \( n \geq  4 \) . Notice that the cone \( C \) of 2-nonnegative curvature operators satisfies the assumptions of Proposition 3.2. We plan to show that the family of closed invariant cones from Proposition 3.2 can be extended to a pinching family. By the above remark it suffices to show that \( {\mathrm{l}}_{a\left( b\right) , b}\left( C\right) \) is contained in the cone of nonnegative curvature operators where \( b \) is the maximal allowed value from Proposition 3.2. In fact then we can extend the family from Proposition 3.2 to a pinching family by defining it on the second part of the interval as a reparametrization of the pinching family \( {\left( C\left( s\right)  \cap  {C}^{\prime }\right) }_{s \in  \lbrack 0,1)} \) where \( {C}^{\prime } \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\mathrm{l}}_{a\left( b\right) , b}\left( C\right) \) .

Let \( \mathrm{R} \in  C \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) . Recall that by (7) we have \( {\mathrm{l}}_{a, b}\left( \mathrm{R}\right)  = \mathrm{R} + {2b}\operatorname{Ric} \land  \mathrm{{id}} + h{\mathrm{R}}_{I} \) for \( h \mathrel{\text{ := }} 2\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {a - b}\right) \) . The smallest eigenvalue of \( \mathrm{R} \) is by a standard estimate larger than or equal to \( - \frac{2\operatorname{tr}\left( \mathrm{R}\right) }{n\left( {n - 1}\right)  - 4} \) . Moreover, since the sum of the two smallest eigenvalues of \( \mathrm{R} \) is nonnegative the smallest eigenvalue of Ric is bounded from below by \( \left( {n - 3}\right) \) times the absolute value of the smallest eigenvalue of \( \mathrm{R} \) . Thus in order to show that \( {\mathrm{l}}_{a, b}\left( \mathrm{R}\right)  \geq  0 \) it is sufficient to prove \( h \geq  \left( {1 - {2b}}\right) \frac{n\left( {n - 1}\right) }{n\left( {n - 1}\right)  - 4} \) . This is equivalent to

\[
\left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2} \geq  \left( {1 - {2b}}\right) \frac{n}{n\left( {n - 1}\right)  - 4}.
\]

By the definition of \( b \) we have \( \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2} = \frac{2}{n}\left( {1 - {2b}}\right) \) . This shows the claim for \( n \geq  4 \) . For \( n = 3 \) , Theorem 3.1 is well known.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( \mathrm{R} \in  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right) \) be a curvature operator of Ricci type, and let \( \bar{\lambda } \) and \( \sigma \) be as in (2). Then

\[
{\mathrm{R}}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}^{\# } = \frac{1}{n - 2}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{0} \land  {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0} + \frac{2\bar{\lambda }}{\left( n - 1\right) }{\operatorname{Ric}}_{0} \land  \operatorname{id} - \frac{2}{{\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}}{\left( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0}^{2}\right) }_{0} \land  \operatorname{id}
\]

\[
+ \frac{{\bar{\lambda }}^{2}}{n - 1}I + \frac{\sigma }{n - 2}I
\]

Moreover

\[
{\left( {\mathrm{R}}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}^{\# }\right) }_{\mathrm{W}} = \frac{1}{n - 2}{\left( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0} \land  {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0}\right) }_{\mathrm{W}}
\]

\[
\operatorname{Ric}\left( {{\mathrm{R}}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}^{\# }}\right)  =  - \frac{2}{n - 2}{\left( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0}^{2}\right) }_{0} + \frac{n - 2}{n - 1}\bar{\lambda }{\operatorname{Ric}}_{0} + {\bar{\lambda }}^{2}\operatorname{id} + \sigma \operatorname{id}.
\]

depends_on.document_title: Christoph Boehm and Burkhard Wilking - Manifolds with Positive Curvature Operators Are Space Forms

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
By equation (3)

\[
\mathrm{R} = {\mathrm{R}}_{I} + {\mathrm{R}}_{{\mathrm{{Ric}}}_{0}} = \frac{\bar{\lambda }}{\left( n - 1\right) }I + \frac{2}{\left( n - 2\right) }{\operatorname{Ric}}_{0} \land  \mathrm{{id}}.
\]

Using the abbreviation \( {\mathrm{R}}_{0} = {\mathrm{R}}_{{\mathrm{{Ric}}}_{0}} \) we have

\[
{\mathrm{R}}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}^{\# } = {\mathrm{R}}_{0}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}_{0}^{\# } + \frac{2\bar{\lambda }}{\left( n - 1\right) }\left( {{\mathrm{R}}_{0} + {\mathrm{R}}_{0}\# I}\right)  + \frac{{\bar{\lambda }}^{2}}{{\left( n - 1\right) }^{2}}\left( {I + {I}^{\# }}\right) .
\]

Since the last two summands are known by Lemma 2.1, we may assume that \( \mathrm{R} = {\mathrm{R}}_{{\mathrm{{Ric}}}_{0}} \) . Let \( {\lambda }_{1},\ldots ,{\lambda }_{n} \) denote the eigenvalues of \( {\mathrm{{Ric}}}_{0} \) corresponding to an orthonormal basis \( {e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{n} \) of \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . The curvature operator \( \mathrm{R} \) is diagonal with respect to \( {e}_{1} \land  {e}_{2},\ldots ,{e}_{n - 1} \land  {e}_{n} \) and we denote by \( {\mathrm{R}}_{ij} = \frac{{\lambda }_{i} + {\lambda }_{j}}{n - 2} \) the corresponding eigenvalues for \( 1 \leq  i < j \leq  n \) . Inspection of (4) shows that also \( {\mathrm{R}}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}^{\# } \) is diagonal with respect to this basis. We have

\[
{\left( {\mathrm{R}}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}^{\# }\right) }_{ij} = {\mathrm{R}}_{ij}^{2} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k \neq  i, j}}{\mathrm{R}}_{ik}{\mathrm{R}}_{jk}
\]

\[
= \frac{{\left( {\lambda }_{i} + {\lambda }_{j}\right) }^{2}}{{\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}} + \frac{1}{{\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k \neq  i, j}}\left( {{\lambda }_{i} + {\lambda }_{k}}\right) \left( {{\lambda }_{j} + {\lambda }_{k}}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{{\lambda }_{i}{\lambda }_{j}}{\left( n - 2\right) } + \frac{{n\sigma } - {\lambda }_{i}^{2} - {\lambda }_{j}^{2}}{{\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}}
\]

as claimed.

The second identity follows immediately from the first. To show the last identity notice that the Ricci tensor of \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0} \land  {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0} \) is given by \( - {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0}^{2} \) . A computation shows the claim.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \( b \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1/2}\right\rbrack \) put

\[
a = \frac{\left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2} + {2b}}{2 + 2\left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}\;\text{ and }\;p = \frac{\left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}{1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}.
\]

Then the set

\[
{\mathrm{l}}_{a, b}\left( \left\{  {\mathrm{R} \in  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right)  \mid  \mathrm{R} \geq  0,\operatorname{Ric} \geq  p\left( b\right) \frac{\operatorname{tr}\left( \operatorname{Ric}\right) }{n}}\right\}  \right)
\]

is invariant under the vector field corresponding to (1). In fact, for \( b \in  (0,1/2\rbrack \) it is transverse to the boundary of the set at all boundary points \( \mathrm{R} \neq  0 \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Put

\[
C\left( p\right)  \mathrel{\text{ := }} \left\{  {\mathrm{R} \in  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right)  \mid  \mathrm{R} \geq  0,\operatorname{Ric} \geq  p\left( b\right) \frac{\operatorname{tr}\left( \operatorname{Ric}\right) }{n}}\right\}  .
\]

It suffices to check that for \( \mathrm{R} \in  C\left( p\right)  \smallsetminus  \{ 0\} \) the pulled back vector field \( {X}_{a, b} \) defined in (9) is in the interior of the tangent cone of \( C\left( p\right) \) at \( \mathrm{R} \) .

In the first step we verify that \( {X}_{a, b} \) is positive definite for \( b \in  (0,1/2\rbrack \) . Since \( {\mathrm{R}}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}^{\# } \) is positive semi-definite, we can establish \( {X}_{a, b} > 0 \) by showing \( {D}_{a, b} > 0 \) . Since by assumption \( \mathrm{R} \in  C\left( p\right) \) we have the following estimate for the eigenvalues of \( {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0} \) :

\[
{\lambda }_{i} \geq   - \left( {1 - p}\right) \bar{\lambda }.
\]

Next, observe that

\[
2\left( {a - b}\right)  = \frac{1 - {2b}}{1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}\left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}.
\]

We use the notation of Theorem 2 and Corollary 2.3. Rewriting \( {d}_{ij} \) gives

(10)

\[
{d}_{ij} = \frac{2a}{1 - p}\left( {\left( {1 - p}\right) \bar{\lambda } + {\lambda }_{i}}\right) \left( {\left( {1 - p}\right) \bar{\lambda } + {\lambda }_{j}}\right)  + {2ap}{\bar{\lambda }}^{2} + {b}^{2}\left( {{\lambda }_{i}^{2} + {\lambda }_{j}^{2}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \frac{n\left( {1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}\right)  - \left( {n - 2}\right) \left( {1 - {2b} + n{b}^{2}}\right) }{\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) \left( {1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}\right) }\sigma {b}^{2}\left( {1 - {2b}}\right)
\]

\[
> \frac{2 + 2\left( {n - 2}\right) b}{\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) \left( {1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}\right) }\sigma {b}^{2}\left( {1 - {2b}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  0\text{ . }
\]

In the second step we must show that the above Ricci pinching is preserved by the ordinary differential equation (1). Let \( \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X}_{a, b}\right) \) denote the Ricci tensor of \( {X}_{a, b} \) . Assume that \( {\lambda }_{i} =  - \left( {1 - p}\right) \bar{\lambda } \) . We have to show that

\[
\operatorname{Ric}{\left( {X}_{a, b}\right) }_{ii} > p\frac{\operatorname{scal}\left( {X}_{a, b}\right) }{n} = p\left( {\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) {\bar{\lambda }}^{2} + \frac{{\left( 1 + \left( n - 2\right) b\right) }^{2}}{1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\sigma }\right)
\]

holds for \( b \in  (0,1/2\rbrack \) . We first observe that by (6)

\[
\operatorname{Ric}{\left( {\mathrm{R}}^{2} + {\mathrm{R}}^{\# }\right) }_{ii} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k \neq  i}}{\operatorname{Ric}}_{kk}{\mathrm{R}}_{kiik} \geq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k \neq  i}}p\bar{\lambda }{\mathrm{R}}_{kiik} = {p}^{2}{\bar{\lambda }}^{2}.
\]

Using formula (10) for \( {d}_{ij} \) and \( {\lambda }_{i} =  - \left( {1 - p}\right) \bar{\lambda } \) we see that

\[
\operatorname{Ric}{\left( {X}_{a, b}\right) }_{ii} \geq  {p}^{2}{\bar{\lambda }}^{2} + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{j \neq  i}}{d}_{ij}
\]

\[
= {p}^{2}{\bar{\lambda }}^{2} + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) {ap}{\bar{\lambda }}^{2} + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}{\left( 1 - p\right) }^{2}{\bar{\lambda }}^{2} + n{b}^{2}\sigma
\]

\[
+ \frac{\left( {n - 1}\right) \sigma {b}^{2}\left( {1 - {2b}}\right) }{\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) \left( {1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}\right) }\left( {2 + 2\left( {n - 2}\right) b}\right) .
\]

By our choice for \( b \) and \( p \) it is straightforward to check that

\[
{p}^{2} + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}{\left( 1 - p\right) }^{2} = p.
\]

This shows that in the asserted inequality the \( {\bar{\lambda }}^{2} \) -terms cancel each other. Since \( \sigma  > 0 \) it remains to verify

\[
n{b}^{2} + \frac{\left( {n - 1}\right) {b}^{2}\left( {1 - {2b}}\right) }{\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) \left( {1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}\right) }\left( {2 + 2\left( {n - 2}\right) b}\right)  > p\frac{{\left( 1 + \left( n - 2\right) b\right) }^{2}}{1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}.
\]

The identity

\[
\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right)  = \frac{1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) b + n\left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}{1 + \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}
\]

shows that this is equivalent to

\[
0 < n\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) b + n\left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2}}\right)  - \left( {n - 2}\right) {\left( 1 + \left( n - 2\right) b\right) }^{2}
\]

\[
+ \left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {1 - {2b}}\right) \left( {2 + 2\left( {n - 2}\right) b}\right)
\]

\[
= {2n} + {2n}\left( {n - 2}\right) b\text{ . }
\]

This shows the claim.

We remark that the above sets remain in fact invariant for all \( b > 0 \) . For \( b \rightarrow   + \infty \) they converge to an invariant set of Einstein curvature operators.

\[
a = \frac{1 + s}{2}\;\text{ and }p = 1 - \frac{4}{n + 2 + {4s}}.

Then the set

\[
{\mathrm{l}}_{a, b}\left( \left\{  {\mathrm{R} \in  {S}_{B}^{2}\left( {\mathfrak{{so}}\left( n\right) }\right)  \mid  \mathrm{R} \geq  0,\operatorname{Ric} \geq  p\left( s\right) \frac{\operatorname{tr}\left( \operatorname{Ric}\right) }{n}}\right\}  \right)
\]

is invariant under the vector field corresponding to (1). In fact, it is transverse to the boundary of the set at all boundary points \( \mathrm{R} \neq  0 \) .

Notice that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{1}{a}{\mathrm{l}}_{a, b}\left( \mathrm{R}\right)  = 2\left( {n - 1}\right) {\mathrm{R}}_{I} \) . Consequently the cones of the lemma converge to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{ + }I \) for \( s \rightarrow  \infty \) .

We first consider the case that the sectional curvature of the nonflat gradient shrinking soliton is not strictly positive. Let us pull back the soliton to its universal cover. Then the pull-back metric is again a nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. By Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1), we know that the pull-back solution splits as the metric product of a two-dimensional nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution and \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since the two-dimensional nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is simply connected, it follows from Theorem 6.2.2 that it must be the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) . Thus, the gradient shrinking soliton must be \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R}/\Gamma \) , a metric quotient of the round cylinder.

For each \( \sigma  \in  \Gamma \) and \( \left( {x, s}\right)  \in  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , we write \( \sigma \left( {x, s}\right)  = \left( {{\sigma }_{1}\left( {x, s}\right) ,{\sigma }_{2}\left( {x, s}\right) }\right)  \in \; {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \sigma \) sends lines to lines, and sends cross spheres to cross spheres, we have \( {\sigma }_{2}\left( {x, s}\right)  = {\sigma }_{2}\left( {y, s}\right) \) , for all \( x, y \in  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) . This says that \( {\sigma }_{2} \) reduces to a function of \( s \) alone on \( \mathbb{R} \) . Moreover, for any \( \left( {x, s}\right) ,\left( {{x}^{\prime },{s}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , since \( \sigma \) preserves the distances between cross spheres \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \{ s\} \) and \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \left\{  {s}^{\prime }\right\} \) , we have \( \left| {{\sigma }_{2}\left( {x, s}\right)  - {\sigma }_{2}\left( {{x}^{\prime },{s}^{\prime }}\right) }\right|  = \left| {s - {s}^{\prime }}\right| \) . So the projection \( {\Gamma }_{2} \) of \( \Gamma \) to the second factor \( \mathbb{R} \) is an isometry subgroup of \( \mathbb{R} \) . If the metric quotient \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R}/\Gamma \) were compact, it would not be \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on sufficiently large scales as \( t \rightarrow   - \infty \) . Thus the metric quotient \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R}/\Gamma \) is noncompact. It follows that \( {\Gamma }_{2} = \{ 1\} \) or \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) . In particular, there is a \( \Gamma \) -invariant cross sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) in the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Denote it by \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \{ 0\} \) . Then \( \Gamma \) acts on the round two-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \{ 0\} \) isometrically without fixed points. This implies \( \Gamma \) is either \( \{ 1\} \) or \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) . Hence we conclude that the gradient shrinking soliton is either the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) where \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) flips both \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) and \( \mathbb{R} \) .

We next consider the case that the gradient shrinking soliton is compact and has strictly positive sectional curvature everywhere. By the proof of Theorem 5.2.1 (see also Remark 5.2.8) we see that the compact gradient shrinking soliton is getting round and tends to a space form (with positive constant curvature) as the time approaches the maximal time \( t = 0 \) . Since the shape of a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton does not change up to reparametrizations and homothetical scalings, the gradient shrinking soliton has to be the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or a metric quotient of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) .

Finally we want to exclude the case that the gradient shrinking soliton is non-compact and has strictly positive sectional curvature everywhere.

Suppose there is a (complete three-dimensional) noncompact \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed gradient shrinking soliton \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) , - \infty  < t < 0 \) , with bounded and positive sectional curvature at each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) and satisfying the equation (6.4.1). Then as in (6.2.25), we have

(6.4.2)

\[
{\nabla }_{i}R = 2{R}_{ij}{\nabla }_{j}f
\]

Fix some \( t < 0 \) , say \( t =  - 1 \) , and consider a long shortest geodesic \( \gamma \left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} \) . Let \( {x}_{0} = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) and \( X\left( s\right)  = \dot{\gamma }\left( s\right) \) . Let \( U\left( 0\right) \) be any unit vector orthogonal to \( \dot{\gamma }\left( 0\right) \) and translate \( U\left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \left( s\right) \) to get a parallel vector field \( U\left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} \) , on \( \gamma \) . Set

\[
\widetilde{U}\left( s\right)  = \left\{  \begin{array}{lll} {sU}\left( s\right) , & \text{ for } & 0 \leq  s \leq  1, \\  U\left( s\right) , & \text{ for } & 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} - 1 \\  \left( {\bar{s} - s}\right) U\left( s\right) , & \text{ for } & \bar{s} - 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s}. \end{array}\right.
\]

It follows from the second variation formula of arclength that

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left( {{\left| \dot{\widetilde{U}}\left( s\right) \right| }^{2} - R\left( {X,\widetilde{U}, X,\widetilde{U}}\right) }\right) {ds} \geq  0.
\]

Since the curvature of the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {-1}\right) \) is bounded, we clearly have

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}R\left( {X, U, X, U}\right) {ds} \leq  \text{ const. }
\]

and then

(6.4.3)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} \leq  \text{ const.. }
\]

Moreover, since the curvature of the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {-1}\right) \) is positive, it follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality that for any unit vector field \( Y \) along \( \gamma \) and orthogonal to \( X\left( { = \dot{\gamma }\left( s\right) }\right) \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, Y\right) \right| }^{2}{ds} \leq  {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) {ds}
\]

\[
\leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds}
\]

\[
\leq  \text{ const. }
\]

and then

(6.4.4)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left| {\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right) }\right| {ds} \leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  \left( {\sqrt{\bar{s}} + 1}\right) .
\]

From (6.4.1) we know

\[
{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{X}f + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \frac{1}{2} = 0
\]

and by integrating this equation we get

\[
X\left( {f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) }\right)  - X\left( {f\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) }\right) }\right)  + {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} - \frac{1}{2}\bar{s} = 0.
\]

Thus by (6.4.3) we deduce

(6.4.5)

\[
\frac{\bar{s}}{2} - \text{ const. } \leq  \langle X,\nabla f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) \rangle  \leq  \frac{\bar{s}}{2} + \text{ const. }
\]

Similarly by integrating (6.4.1) and using (6.4.4) we can deduce

(6.4.6)

\[
\left| {\langle Y,\nabla f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) \rangle }\right|  \leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  \left( {\sqrt{\bar{s}} + 1}\right) .
\]

These two inequalities tell us that at large distances from the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) the function \( f \) has no critical point, and its gradient makes a small angle with the gradient of the distance function from \( {x}_{0} \) .

Now from (6.4.2) we see that at large distances from \( {x}_{0}, R \) is strictly increasing along the gradient curves of \( f \) , in particular

\[
\bar{R} = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{\left( -1\right) }\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x, - 1}\right)  > 0.
\]

Let us choose a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{k}, - 1}\right) \) where \( R\left( {{x}_{k}, - 1}\right)  \rightarrow  \bar{R} \) . By the noncol-lapsing assumption we can take a limit along this sequence of points of the gradient soliton and get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution defined on \( - \infty  < t < 0 \) . By Proposition 6.1.2, we deduce that the limiting ancient \( \kappa \) -solution splits off a line. Since the soliton has positive sectional curvature, we know from Gromoll-Meyer [52] that it is orientable. Then it follows from Theorem 6.2.2 that the limiting solution is the shrinking round infinite cylinder with scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) at time \( t =  - 1 \) . Since the limiting solution exists on \( \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) , we conclude that \( \bar{R} \leq  1 \) . Hence

\[
R\left( {x, - 1}\right)  < 1
\]

when the distance from \( x \) to the fixed \( {x}_{0} \) is large enough on the gradient shrinking soliton.

Let us consider the level surface \( \{ f = a\} \) of \( f \) . The second fundamental form of the level surface is given by

\[
{h}_{ij} = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{i}\left( \frac{\nabla f}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\right) ,{e}_{j}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f/\left| {\nabla f}\right| ,\;i, j = 1,2,
\]

where \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}\right\} \) is an orthonormal basis of the level surface. By (6.4.1), we have

\[
{\nabla }_{{e}_{i}}{\nabla }_{{e}_{i}}f = \frac{1}{2} - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{i}}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2} - \frac{R}{2} > 0,\;i = 1,2,
\]

since for a three-manifold the positivity of sectional curvature is equivalent to \( R \geq \) 2Ric. It then follows from the first variation formula that

(6.4.7)

\[
\frac{d}{da}\operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}  = {\int }_{\{ f = a\} }\operatorname{div}\left( \frac{\nabla f}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {\int }_{\{ f = a\} }\frac{1}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\left( {1 - R}\right)
\]

\[
> {\int }_{\{ f = a\} }\frac{1}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\left( {1 - \bar{R}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  0
\]

for \( a \) large enough. We conclude that Area \( \{ f = a\} \) strictly increases as \( a \) increases. From (6.4.5) we see that for \( s \) large enough

\[
\left| {\frac{df}{ds} - \frac{s}{2}}\right|  \leq  \text{ const., }
\]

and then

\[
\left| {f - \frac{{s}^{2}}{4}}\right|  \leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  \left( {s + 1}\right) .
\]

Thus we get from (6.4.7)

\[
\frac{d}{da}\operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}  > \frac{1 - \bar{R}}{2\sqrt{a}}\operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}
\]

for \( a \) large enough. This implies that

\[
\log \operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}  > \left( {1 - \bar{R}}\right) \sqrt{a} - \text{ const. }
\]

for \( a \) large enough. But it is clear from (6.4.7) that Area \( \{ f = a\} \) is uniformly bounded from above by the area of the round sphere of scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) for all large \( a \) . Thus we deduce that \( \bar{R} = 1 \) . So

(6.4.8)

\[
\text{ Area }\{ f = a\}  < {8\pi }
\]

for a large enough.

Denote by \( X \) the unit normal vector to the level surface \( \{ f = a\} \) . By using the Gauss equation and (6.4.1), the intrinsic curvature of the level surface \( \{ f = a\} \) can be computed as

(6.4.9) intrinsic curvature

\[
= {R}_{1212} + \det \left( {h}_{ij}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left( {R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{\det \left( {\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) }\right) }{{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{2}\left( {R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{1}{4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{\left( \operatorname{tr}\left( \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \right) \right) }^{2}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left( {R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{1}{4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{\left( 1 - \left( R - \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) \right) }^{2}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {1 - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \left( {1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{{\left( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) }^{2}}{2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
< \frac{1}{2}
\]

for sufficiently large \( a \) , since \( \left( {1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  > 0 \) and \( \left| {\nabla f}\right| \) is large when \( a \) is large. Thus the combination of (6.4.8) and (6.4.9) gives a contradiction to the Gauss-Bonnet formula.

Therefore we have proved the lemma.
