knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Let \( s\left( t\right) \) be the function defined in the proof of Theorem 12.35. Since \( \mathcal{K}\left( t\right) \) changes continuously in \( t, s\left( t\right) \) is a continuous function. We shall show that for some constant \( C < \infty ,\frac{{d}_{ + }s}{dt} \leq  {Cs} \) whenever \( s\left( t\right)  > 0 \) ; the theorem then follows from Exercise 10.28 since \( s\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) .

We shall compute \( \frac{{d}_{ \pm  }s}{dt} \) at \( {t}_{0} \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) where \( s\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) . From the growth assumption on \( u \) and (12.11), there exists \( {x}_{0} \in  \mathcal{M} \) such that

\[
s\left( {t}_{0}\right)  = {\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - {\varepsilon \phi }\left( {{x}_{0}, t}\right)  = d\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) ,\mathcal{K}{\left( {t}_{0}\right) }_{{x}_{0}}}\right)  - {\varepsilon \phi }\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) .
\]

For \( h > 0 \) , since \( s\left( {{t}_{0} - h}\right)  \geq  {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0} - h}\right) }\right)  - {\varepsilon \phi }\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0} - h}\right) \) , we have

\[
\frac{{d}_{ + }s}{dt} \leq  \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{h \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}\frac{{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0} - h}\right) }\right) }{h} - \varepsilon \frac{\partial \phi }{\partial t}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) .
\]

From the PDE \( \left( {10.24}\right) \) (we are using \( X\left( t\right)  = 0 \) and \( F\left( {u, t}\right)  = F\left( u\right) \) ),

\[
u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0} - h}\right)  = u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {h\Delta u}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  + o\left( h\right) .
\]

Since \( {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( \cdot \right) \) is a Lipschitz function on \( {\mathcal{V}}_{x} \) (with Lipschitz constant 1), we have

\[
\frac{\left| {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0} - h\right) \right)  - {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right)  - h\Delta u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right)  - hF\left( u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) \right) \right) \right| }{h}
\]

\[
\leq  o\left( 1\right) \text{ . }
\]

Hence

\[
\frac{{d}_{ + }s}{dt} \leq   - \varepsilon \left( {{\Delta \phi } + {A\phi }}\right) \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{h \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}\frac{{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {h\Delta u}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right) }{h}.
\]

Next we claim that for any \( {\varepsilon }_{1} > 0 \) , when \( h \) is small enough, we have

(12.50)

\[
{\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {h\Delta u}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq   - {\varepsilon }_{1}h - {\varepsilon \Delta \phi }\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  + {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right) .
\]

To see the claim, from the convexity of the distance function \( {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h} \) we have for \( h > 0 \)

\[
{\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {h\Delta u}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right)  - \left\langle  {{\Delta u}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) ,\nabla {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u}_{1}\right) }\right\rangle   \cdot  h,
\]

where \( {u}_{1} \Doteq  u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) and \( \langle \) , \( \rangle {istheinnerproductonV} \) . We shall show that

(12.51)

\[
\left\langle  {{\Delta u}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) ,\nabla {\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right\rangle   \leq  {\varepsilon \Delta \phi }\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) .
\]

Since \( \nabla {\rho }_{t}\left( w\right) \) is a continuous function of \( \left( {w, t}\right) \) (see Lemma 10.53(iii)), given \( {\varepsilon }_{1} > 0 \) , we can choose \( h \) small enough so that

\[
\left\langle  {{\Delta u}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) ,\nabla {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u}_{1}\right) }\right\rangle   \leq  {\varepsilon }_{1} + {\varepsilon \Delta \phi }\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) ,
\]

which will imply the claim.

Now inequality (12.50) implies that we can drop the Laplacian term in (12.49):(12.52)

\[
\frac{{d}_{ + }s}{dt} \leq  \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{h \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}\frac{{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right) }{h} - {\varepsilon A\phi }.
\]

Given \( h > 0 \) small enough, we choose \( {v}_{h} \in  \mathcal{K}{\left( {t}_{0} - h\right) }_{{x}_{0}} \) (the closest point) so that

(12.53)

\[
{\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right)  = {\left| u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right)  - hF\left( u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) \right)  - {v}_{h}\right| }_{{\mathcal{V}}_{{x}_{0}}},
\]

where \( {\left| \cdot \right| }_{{\mathcal{V}}_{{x}_{0}}} \) denotes the norm on \( {\mathcal{V}}_{{x}_{0}} \) . This implies that

\[
{\left| u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right)  - {v}_{h}\right| }_{{\mathcal{V}}_{{x}_{0}}} = {\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  + o\left( 1\right) .
\]

By (12.53) and the fact that \( {\rho }_{{t}_{0}} \) has Lipschitz constant 1, we may bound the numerator of the RHS of (12.52) as follows:

\[
{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - {\left| u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right)  - hF\left( {v}_{h}\right)  - {v}_{h}\right| }_{{\mathcal{V}}_{{x}_{0}}}
\]

\[
+ {\left| hF\left( {v}_{h}\right)  - hF\left( u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) \right) \right| }_{{\mathcal{V}}_{{x}_{0}}}
\]

\[
\leq  {\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{hF}\left( {v}_{h}\right)  + {v}_{h}}\right)  + {\left. h\left| F\left( {v}_{h}\right)  - F\left( u\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) \right) \right| \right| }_{{\mathcal{V}}_{{x}_{0}}}
\]

(12.54)

\[
\leq  {\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{hF}\left( {v}_{h}\right)  + {v}_{h}}\right)  + {hC}{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  + o\left( h\right) ,
\]

where to obtain the last inequality we have used the locally Lipschitz property of \( F \) .

Let \( {U}_{{v}_{h}} \) be the solution of the ODE (10.63) with initial value

\[
{U}_{{v}_{h}}\left( {{t}_{0} - h}\right)  = {v}_{h} \in  \mathcal{K}{\left( {t}_{0} - h\right) }_{{x}_{0}}.
\]

Then

\[
{\left| {U}_{{v}_{h}}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  - \left( {v}_{h} + hF\left( {v}_{h}\right) \right) \right| }_{{\mathcal{V}}_{{x}_{0}}} \leq  o\left( h\right) .
\]

Since the sets \( \mathcal{K}{\left( t\right) }_{{x}_{0}} \) are preserved under the ODE, we have \( {U}_{{v}_{h}}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \in \; \mathcal{K}{\left( {t}_{0}\right) }_{{x}_{0}} \) , and hence

(12.55)

\[
\text{ 55) }{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{v}_{h} + {hF}\left( {v}_{h}\right) }\right)  \leq  {\left| {U}_{{v}_{h}}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  - \left( {v}_{h} + hF\left( {v}_{h}\right) \right) \right| }_{{\mathcal{V}}_{{x}_{0}}} \leq  o\left( h\right) \text{ . }
\]

Hence, by (12.54) and (12.55), we have

\[
{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - {\rho }_{{t}_{0} - h}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {hF}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) }\right)  \leq  {hC}{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  + o\left( h\right) .
\]

Combining this with (10.57), we have proved

\[
\frac{{d}_{ + }s}{dt} \leq  C{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - {\varepsilon A\phi } = {Cs}\left( {t}_{0}\right)
\]

when we choose \( A \geq  C \) (while \( s\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) ). The version of Theorem 10.16 where \( X\left( t\right)  = 0, F\left( {u, t}\right)  = F\left( u\right) \) , and the fiberwise convex sets depend continuously on time has been proved.

Finally we give a proof of (12.51). Note that the function \( {\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - \; {\varepsilon \phi }\left( {x, t}\right) \) attains its maximum at \( x = {x}_{0} \) . Hence if \( {\rho }_{{t}_{0}} \) is \( {C}^{2} \) at \( u\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , then at \( {x}_{0} \) we have

\[
0 \geq  \Delta \left( {{\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\left( {u\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right)  - {\varepsilon \phi }\left( {x, t}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= \operatorname{Hess}\left( {\rho }_{{t}_{0}}\right) \left( {\nabla u,\nabla u}\right) \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  + \left\langle  {\nabla {\rho }_{{t}_{0}},{\Delta u}}\right\rangle  \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {\varepsilon \Delta \phi }\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \left\langle  {\nabla {\rho }_{{t}_{0}},{\Delta u}}\right\rangle  \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  - {\varepsilon \Delta \phi }\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

since \( {\rho }_{{t}_{0}} \) is a convex function. Note that when \( {\rho }_{{t}_{0}} \) is not \( {C}^{2} \) , then the support function argument in Section 9 of Chapter 7 of Part I of this volume will apply, still giving the above inequality since \( {\rho }_{{t}_{0}} \) is \( {C}^{1} \) .

Proof. Given any point \( y \in  \mathcal{U} \) , let \( \Omega  \subset  \mathcal{U} \) be a connected open set such that \( \bar{\Omega } \) is a compact manifold with smooth boundary and \( \Omega \) contains both \( {x}_{0} \) and \( y \) . Let \( {\varphi }_{k} : \bar{\Omega } \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be a smooth nonnegative function satisfying

\[
k{\varphi }_{k}\left( x\right)  \leq  {\phi }_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  \bar{\Omega }, k{\varphi }_{k}\left( {x}_{0}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2}{\phi }_{k}\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) , and \( {\varphi }_{k} = 0 \) on \( \partial \Omega \) . It is easy to see that such a function \( {\varphi }_{k} \) exists. For some constant \( A > 0 \) to be determined later, let \( f : \bar{\Omega } \times  \lbrack 0, T) \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) be the solution to the following initial-boundary value problem on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) (the existence of the solution follows from the same reason given in the proof of Proposition 12.47):

(12.62)

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} = {\Delta f} + {Xf} - {Af}
\]

\[
{\left. f\right| }_{\partial \Omega  \times  \lbrack 0, T)} = 0\;\text{ and }\;f\left( {x,0}\right)  = {\varphi }_{k}\left( x\right) .
\]

Note that \( {\phi }_{k}\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right)  > 0 \) implies \( {\varphi }_{k}\left( {x}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) . By the strong maximum principle for scalars (applying Theorem 12.40 to \( - f \) ), we have \( f > 0 \) on \( \Omega  \times  (0, T\rbrack \) . Also, by the weak maximum principle (Theorem 10.2), we have

\[
f\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \mathop{\max }\limits_{\bar{\Omega }}{\varphi }_{k}\left( \cdot \right)  \leq  \frac{1}{k}\mathop{\max }\limits_{\bar{\Omega }}{\phi }_{k}\left( {x,0}\right) \text{ on }\Omega  \times  (0, T\rbrack .
\]

Let \( \widetilde{h} \) be the section of \( \mathcal{V} = \operatorname{Hom}\left( {\mathcal{W},\mathcal{W}}\right) \) as in (12.41). Define

(12.63)

\[
\bar{u}\left( {x, t}\right)  \Doteq  u\left( {x, t}\right)  + \left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} - f\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \widetilde{h}\left( x\right)
\]

and

\[
{\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \Doteq  \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{\left\{  {{e}_{1},\ldots ,{e}_{k}}\right\}  \text{ orthonormal }}}\left( {\bar{u}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  + \cdots  + \bar{u}\left( {{e}_{k},{e}_{k}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {\phi }_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  + k\left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} - f\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) ,
\]

where \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) . We claim that for \( \varepsilon \) sufficiently small, \( {\bar{\phi }}_{k} > 0 \) on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . The proposition will follow from the claim easily. Taking the limit as \( \varepsilon  \rightarrow  0 \) , we obtain \( {\phi }_{k} \geq  {kf} \) in \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) ; in particular, \( {\phi }_{k}\left( {y, t}\right)  > 0 \) for any \( t > 0 \) since \( y \in  \Omega \) and \( f\left( {y, t}\right)  > 0 \) . Since \( y \in  \mathcal{U} \) is arbitrary, the proposition is proved assuming the claim.

We now prove the claim by contradiction. If the claim is false, since by the definition of \( f\left( {x, t}\right) \) we have \( {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  > 0 \) in \( \Omega \) and \( {\left. {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( x, t\right) \right| }_{\partial \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack  } > 0 \) , there exists \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  \in  \Omega  \times  (0, T\rbrack \) such that \( {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) and \( {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {0,{t}_{1}}\right) \) . Let \( \left\{  {{E}_{1}^{0},\ldots ,{E}_{k}^{0}}\right\}   \in  {\mathcal{W}}_{{x}_{1}} \) be orthonormal vectors such that

\[
\bar{u}\left( {{E}_{1}^{0},{E}_{1}^{0}}\right)  + \cdots  + \bar{u}\left( {{E}_{k}^{0},{E}_{k}^{0}}\right)  = 0
\]

at \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \) . As in Section 2 of Chapter 10, we extend each \( {E}_{i}^{0} \) in space and time to a local vector field \( {E}_{i} \) by parallel translating \( {E}_{i}^{0} \) along geodesics emanating from \( {x}_{1} \) (with respect to \( \nabla \left( {t}_{1}\right) \) ) and taking \( {E}_{i} \) to be constant in time. Then \( \nabla {E}_{i}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0,\Delta {E}_{i}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) , and \( \frac{\partial {E}_{i}}{\partial t}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Define

\[
{\psi }_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \Doteq  \bar{u}\left( {x, t}\right) \left( {{E}_{1},{E}_{1}}\right)  + \cdots  + \bar{u}\left( {x, t}\right) \left( {{E}_{k},{E}_{k}}\right)
\]

in a neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \) . We have \( {\psi }_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  {\bar{\phi }}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  0 \) for \( t \leq  {t}_{1} \) and \( {\psi }_{k}\left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Hence by the second derivative test we have at \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \)

\[
\frac{\partial {\psi }_{k}}{\partial t} \leq  0,\;\nabla {\psi }_{k} = 0,\;\text{ and }\;\Delta {\psi }_{k} \geq  0.
\]

Using (12.58),(12.62), and the properties of \( {E}_{i} \) and \( \widetilde{h} \) , we compute at \( \left( {{x}_{1},{t}_{1}}\right) \)

\[
0 \geq  \frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\psi }_{k} - \Delta {\psi }_{k} - {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }{\psi }_{k}
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left( {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \Delta  - {\nabla }_{X\left( t\right) }}\right) \bar{u}}\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)
\]

\[
= \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)  + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left( {\beta \left( {u, t}\right)  - \beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right) }\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {Ak}\left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} + f}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Since \( \beta \) satisfies the null-eigenvector assumption, \( \beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)  \geq  0 \) . Hence we have

(12.64)

\[
0 \geq  \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{k}\left( {\beta \left( {u, t}\right)  - \beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right) }\right) \left( {{E}_{i}^{0},{E}_{i}^{0}}\right)  + {Ak}\left( {\varepsilon {e}^{At} + f}\right) .
\]

Since \( \bar{\Omega } \) is compact, there exists \( {L}_{1} < \infty \) such that \( \left| u\right|  \leq  {L}_{1} \) and \( \left| f\right|  \leq  {L}_{1} \) on \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {0, T}\right\rbrack \) . When \( \varepsilon {e}^{AT} \leq  1 \) , we have from (12.63) that \( \left| \bar{u}\right|  \leq  {L}_{1} + \operatorname{rank}\mathcal{W} \) . Hence, by the locally Lipschitz assumption on \( \beta \) , there is a constant \( {K}_{1} = \; {K}_{1}\left( {{L}_{1},\operatorname{rank}\mathcal{W}}\right) \) such that

\[
\beta \left( {u, t}\right)  - \beta \left( {\bar{u}, t}\right)  \geq   - {K}_{1}\left| {\varepsilon {e}^{At} - f}\right| \widetilde{h}\left( x\right) .
\]

Applying this to (12.64), we have

\[
0 \geq  \left( {A - {K}_{1}}\right) k\left( {{e}^{At} + f}\right) .
\]

We obtain a contradiction by first choosing \( A > {K}_{1} \) and then choosing \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,{e}^{-{AT}}}\right\rbrack \) . The claim is proved and the proposition follows.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: WPIC, WPIC1, and WPIC2 Curvature Conditions
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An algebraic curvature operator \( R \) is said to be WPIC (weakly positive isotropic curvature) if for any orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) , we have

\[
{R}_{1313} + {R}_{1414} + {R}_{2323} + {R}_{2424} - 2{R}_{1234} \geq  0. \tag{1.1}
\]

\( R \) is said to be WPIC1 if for any orthonormal four-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and any \( \lambda  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) ,

\[
{R}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{1414} + {R}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{2424} - {2\lambda }{R}_{1234} \geq  0. \tag{1.2}
\]

Moreover \( R \) is said to be WPIC2 if for any orthonormal 4-frame \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and any \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) .

\[
{R}_{1313} + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{1414} + {\mu }^{2}{R}_{2323} + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}{R}_{2424} - {2\lambda \mu }{R}_{1234} \geq  0. \tag{1.3}
\]

We call \( {C}_{PIC},{C}_{PIC1},{C}_{PIC2} \) the cones consisting of algebraic curvature operators that satisfy WPIC, WPIC1 or WPIC2 respectively. Moreover, \( R \) is said to be PIC, PIC1 or PIC2 if it’s contained in the interior of \( {C}_{PIC1},{C}_{PIC1} \) or \( {C}_{PIC2} \) respectively. A manifold \( M \) is a PIC, PIC1 or PIC2 manifold if there exists a metric \( g \) on \( M \) such that its curvature operator is PIC, PIC1 or PIC2 respectively.

We may assume \( {\lambda }_{1} \leq  {\lambda }_{2} \leq  \cdots  \leq  {\lambda }_{n} \) are eigenvalues for \( {Ric} \) , and \( \bar{\lambda } = \frac{scal}{n} = \frac{1}{n}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i} \) . Then we have

\[
{\left| {\operatorname{Ric}}_{0}\right| }^{2} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 1}}^{n}{\left( {\lambda }_{i} - \bar{\lambda }\right) }^{2}
\]

\[
\geq  {\left( {\lambda }_{1} - \bar{\lambda }\right) }^{2} + {\left( {\lambda }_{2} - \bar{\lambda }\right) }^{2} + \left( {n - 2}\right) {\left( \frac{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 3}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i}}{n - 2} - \bar{\lambda }\right) }^{2}.
\]

Now, if we replace \( R \) by \( R + c\mathrm{{id}} \land  \mathrm{{id}} \) for some real number \( c \) , then the two sides of 3.6 remain the same. By the homogeneity of the inequality, we can assume without loss of generality that \( {\lambda }_{1} =  - 1,{\lambda }_{2} = 0 \) . Denote \( \nu  = \frac{1}{n - 2}\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i = 3}}^{n}{\lambda }_{i} \) , then \( \nu  \geq  0 \) and \( \bar{\lambda } = \frac{1}{n}\left( {\left( {n - 2}\right) \nu  - 1}\right) \) , we calculate that

\[
{\left| Ri{c}_{0}\right| }^{2} \geq  \frac{{\left( \left( n - 2\right) \nu  + \left( n - 1\right) \right) }^{2}}{{n}^{2}} + \frac{{\left( \left( n - 2\right) \nu  - 1\right) }^{2}}{{n}^{2}} + \left( {n - 2}\right) \frac{{\left( 2\nu  + 1\right) }^{2}}{{n}^{2}}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{{n}^{2}}\left( {{2n}\left( {n - 2}\right) {\nu }^{2} + {2n}\left( {n - 2}\right) \nu  + n\left( {n - 1}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{n - 1}{n}
\]

The assertion follows.

{P}_{1} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}b}\left( \frac{2\left( {n - 1}\right) \gamma \left( {1 - {2b}}\right) }{{n}^{2}}\right)  < \frac{2\left( {n - 1}\right) }{{n}^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}\gamma }{\mathrm{d}b} < \frac{1}{n + 1} \leq  \frac{1}{10},
\]

since the term \( 1 - {2b} \) is positive and decreasing in \( b \) and \( \frac{\mathrm{d}\gamma }{\mathrm{d}b} < \frac{1}{2} \) . Now, for the term \( {P}_{2} \) , we have

\[
{P}_{2} = \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}b}\left( \frac{2\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {1 + \gamma }\right) \left( {{n}^{2}{b}^{2} - 2\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {a - b}\right) \left( {1 - {2b}}\right) }\right) }{{n}^{2}\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}b}\left( \frac{4\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {1 + \gamma }\right) \left( {\left( {{2n} - 1}\right) {b}^{2} + \left( {{3n} - 2}\right) \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{3} + \left( {n - 1}\right) {\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}{b}^{4}}\right) }{{n}^{2}\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) \left( {2 + \left( {n - 3}\right) b}\right) }\right) .
\]

Now notice that \( 1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a \) and \( 2 + \left( {n - 3}\right) b \) are both positive and increasing in \( b \) , combining with \( 0 < b \leq  {b}_{\max } = \frac{1}{{2n} + 2} \) and \( \frac{\mathrm{d}\gamma }{\mathrm{d}b} < \frac{1}{2} \) , we have

\[
{P}_{2} \leq  \frac{4\left( {n - 1}\right) }{{n}^{2}\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) \left( {2 + \left( {n - 3}\right) b}\right) }\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}b}\left( {\left( {1 + \gamma }\right) \left( {\left( {{2n} - 1}\right) {b}^{2} + \left( {{3n} - 2}\right) \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{3} + \left( {n - 1}\right) {\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}{b}^{4}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
< \frac{4\left( {n - 1}\right) }{{n}^{2}\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) \left( {2 + \left( {n - 3}\right) b}\right) }\left( {\left( {1 + \gamma }\right) \left( {2\left( {{2n} - 1}\right) b + 3\left( {{3n} - 2}\right) \left( {n - 2}\right) {b}^{2} + 4\left( {n - 1}\right) {\left( n - 2\right) }^{2}{b}^{3}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
+ \frac{2\left( {n - 1}\right) }{{n}^{2}\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) a}\right) \left( {2 + \left( {n - 3}\right) b}\right) }\left( {{2n}{b}^{2} + 3{n}^{2}{b}^{3} + {n}^{3}{b}^{4}}\right) )
\]

\[
< \frac{4\left( {n - 1}\right) }{{n}^{2}\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) b}\right) \left( {2 + \left( {n - 3}\right) b}\right) }\left( {{4nb} + 9{n}^{2}{b}^{2} + 4{n}^{3}{b}^{3}}\right)  + \frac{n - 1}{{n}^{2}}\left( {{2n}{b}^{2} + 3{n}^{2}{b}^{3} + {n}^{3}{b}^{4}}\right)
\]

\[
< \frac{4\left( {{4b} + {9n}{b}^{2} + 4{n}^{2}{b}^{3}}\right) }{\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) b}\right) )\left( {2 + \left( {n - 3}\right) b}\right) } + \left( {2{b}^{2} + {3n}{b}^{3} + {n}^{2}{b}^{4}}\right) \text{ . }
\]

We claim that

\[
\frac{4\left( {{4b} + {9n}{b}^{2} + 4{n}^{2}{b}^{3}}\right) }{\left( {1 + 2\left( {n - 1}\right) b}\right) )\left( {2 + \left( {n - 3}\right) b}\right) } < \frac{4}{9}.
\]

In fact, the above equation is equivalent to

\[
{36}{n}^{2}{b}^{3} + \left( {{81n} - 2\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {n - 3}\right) }\right) {b}^{2} + \left( {{42} - {5n}}\right) b < 2,
\]

and we verify directly that

\[
{36}{n}^{2}{b}^{3} + \left( {{81n} - 2\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {n - 3}\right) }\right) {b}^{2} + \left( {{42} - {5n}}\right) b \leq  {36}{n}^{2}{b}_{\max }^{3} + \left( {{81} - 2\left( {n - 1}\right) \left( {n - 3}\right) }\right) {b}_{\max }^{2} < 2,
\]

hence the claim is true.

Moreover we can check that

\[
2{b}^{2} + {3n}{b}^{3} + {n}^{2}{b}^{4} < \frac{1}{100}.
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}\rho }{\mathrm{d}b} = 1 - {P}_{1} - {P}_{2} > 1 - \frac{1}{10} - \frac{4}{9} - \frac{1}{100} > \frac{4}{9},
\]

the assertion follows.

For the second statement: we first calculate that

\[

\]

hence the statement is equivalent to the following :

\[

(3.4)

For LHS, observe that

\[

\]

By Lemma 3.4, we obtain

\[
{LHS} \leq  {\left( \frac{n - 3}{n - 4}\right) }^{2}g\left( b\right)  \leq  {\left( \frac{n - 3}{n - 4}\right) }^{2}g\left( {b}_{\max }\right) .
\]

Now we show that RHS is strictly decreasing in \( b \) . Notice that \( \rho  < b \) and by Lemma 3.5, \( \frac{\mathrm{d}\rho }{\mathrm{d}b} > \frac{4}{9} \) , we have

\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}b}\left( \frac{b\left( {2 + \left( {n - 2}\right) b}\right) }{{\rho }^{3}}\right)  = \frac{1}{{\rho }^{4}}\left( {\left( {2 + 2\left( {n - 2}\right) b}\right) \rho  - 3\left( {2 + \left( {n - 2}\right) b}\right) b\frac{\mathrm{d}\rho }{\mathrm{d}b}}\right)
\]

\[
< \frac{b}{{\rho }^{4}}\left( {\left( {2 + 2\left( {n - 2}\right) b}\right)  - \frac{4}{3}\left( {2 + \left( {n - 2}\right) b}\right) }\right)  = \frac{b}{{\rho }^{4}}\left( {-\frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3}\left( {n - 2}\right) b}\right)  < 0.

We can now verify directly that, for \( 9 \leq  n \leq  {11} \) and \( {b}_{max} = \frac{1}{{2n} + 2} \) ,

\[

\]

\[

\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) be a generalized Ricci flow satisfying Assumptions (1) - (7) with initial conditions \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . Suppose that for some \( T \) the time-slice \( {M}_{T} \) of this generalized flow satisfies Thurston’s Geometriza-tion Conjecture. Then the same is true for the manifold \( {M}_{t} \) for any \( t \leq  T \) , and in particular M satisfies Thurston's Geometrization Conjecture. In addition:

(1) If for some \( T > 0 \) the manifold \( {M}_{T} \) is empty, then \( M \) is a connected sum of manifolds diffeomorphic to 2-sphere bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) and 3- dimensional space-forms, i.e., compact 3-manifolds that admit a metric of constant positive curvature.

(2) If for some \( T > 0 \) the manifold \( {M}_{T} \) is empty and if \( M \) is connected and simply connected, then \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3} \) .

(3) If for some \( T > 0 \) the manifold \( {M}_{T} \) is empty and if \( M \) has finite fundamental group, then M is a 3-dimensional space-form.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Suppose that \( {M}_{T} \) satisfies the Thurston Geometrization Conjecture and that \( {t}_{0} \) is the largest surgery time \( \leq  T \) . (If there is no such surgery time then \( {M}_{T} \) is diffeomorphic to \( M \) and the result is established.) Let \( {T}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} \) be sufficiently close to \( {t}_{0} \) so that \( {t}_{0} \) is the only surgery time in the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{T}^{\prime }, T}\right\rbrack \) . Then according to the previous proposition \( {M}_{{T}^{\prime }} \) is obtained from \( {M}_{T} \) by first taking the disjoint union of \( {M}_{T} \) and copies of 2-sphere bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) and 3-dimensional space forms. In the Thurston Geometriza-tion Conjecture the first step is to decompose the manifold as a connected sum of prime 3-manifolds and then to treat each prime piece independently. Clearly, the prime decomposition of \( {M}_{{T}^{\prime }} \) is obtained from the prime decomposition of \( {M}_{T} \) by adding a disjoint union with 2-sphere bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) and 3-dimensional space forms. By definition any 3-dimensional space-form satisfies Thurston's Geometrization Conjecture. Since any diffeomorphism of \( {S}^{2} \) to itself is isotopic to either the identity or to the antipodal map, there are two diffeomorphism types of 2-sphere bundles over \( {S}^{1} : {S}^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \) and the non-orientable 2-sphere bundle over \( {S}^{1} \) . Each is obtained from \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) by gluing the ends together via an isometry of the round metric on \( {S}^{2} \) . Hence, each has a homogeneous geometry modeled on \( {S}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , and hence satisfies Thurston’s Geometrization Conjecture. This proves that if \( {M}_{T} \) satisfies this conjecture, then so does \( {M}_{{T}^{\prime }} \) . Continuing this way by induction, using the fact that there are only finitely many surgery times completes the proof of the first statement.

Statement (1) is proved analogously. Suppose that \( {M}_{T} \) is a disjoint union of connected sums of 2-sphere bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) and 3-dimensional space-forms. Let \( {t}_{0} \) be the largest surgery time \( \leq  T \) and let \( {T}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} \) be sufficiently close to \( {t}_{0} \) . (As before, if there is no such \( {t}_{0} \) then \( {M}_{T} \) is diffeomorphic to \( M \) and the result is established.) Then it is clear from the previous proposition that \( {M}_{{T}^{\prime }} \) is also a disjoint union of connected sums of 3-dimensional space-forms and 2-sphere bundles over \( {S}^{1} \) . Induction as in the previous case completes the argument for this case.

The last two statements are immediate from this one.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
It suffices to show the following general result:

There exists a constant \( c > 0 \) depending only on the dimension, and constants \( {C}_{q} \) depending only on the dimension and \( q \) and bounds \( {B}_{j} \) on the curvature and its derivatives for \( j \leq  q \) where \( \left| {{D}^{j}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {B}_{j} \) , so that for any metric \( {g}_{k\ell } \) in geodesic coordinates in the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) , we have

\[
\frac{1}{2}{I}_{k\ell } \leq  {g}_{k\ell } \leq  2{I}_{k\ell }
\]

and

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{1}}}\cdots \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{q}}}{g}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  {C}_{q}
\]

where \( {I}_{k\ell } \) is the Euclidean metric.

Suppose we are given a metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( x\right) d{x}^{i}d{x}^{j} \) in geodesic coordinates in the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) as in Claim 1. Then by definition every line through the origin is a geodesic (parametrized proportional to arc length) and \( {g}_{ij} = {I}_{ij} \) at the origin. Also, the Gauss Lemma says that the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) is in geodesic coordinates if and only if \( {g}_{ij}{x}^{i} = {I}_{ij}{x}^{i} \) . Note in particular that in geodesic coordinates

\[
{\left| x\right| }^{2} = {g}_{ij}{x}^{i}{x}^{j} = {I}_{ij}{x}^{i}{x}^{j}
\]

is unambiguously defined. Also, in geodesic coordinates we have \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) , and all the first derivatives for \( {g}_{jk} \) vanish at the origin.

Introduce the symmetric tensor

\[
{A}_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}{x}^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{k}}{g}_{ij}.
\]

Since we have \( {g}_{jk}{x}^{k} = {I}_{jk}{x}^{k} \) , we get

\[
{x}^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{g}_{jk} = {I}_{ij} - {g}_{ij} = {x}^{k}\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{j}}{g}_{ik}
\]

and hence from the formula for \( {\Gamma }_{jk}^{i} \)

\[
{x}^{j}{\Gamma }_{jk}^{i} = {g}^{i\ell }{A}_{k\ell }
\]

Hence \( {A}_{k\ell }{x}^{k} = 0 \) . Let \( {D}_{i} \) be the covariant derivative with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) . Then

\[
{D}_{i}{x}^{k} = {I}_{i}^{k} + {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k}{x}^{j} = {I}_{i}^{k} + {g}^{k\ell }{A}_{i\ell }.
\]

Introduce the potential function

\[
P = {\left| x\right| }^{2}/2 = \frac{1}{2}{g}_{ij}{x}^{i}{x}^{j}.
\]

We can use the formulas above to compute

\[
{D}_{i}P = {g}_{ij}{x}^{j}.
\]

Also we get

\[
{D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij}.
\]

The defining equation for \( P \) gives

\[
{g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}P = {2P}.
\]

If we take the covariant derivative of this equation we get

\[
{g}^{k\ell }{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P{D}_{\ell }P = {D}_{j}P
\]

which is equivalent to \( {A}_{jk}{x}^{k} = 0 \) . But if we take the covariant derivative again we get

\[
{g}^{k\ell }{D}_{i}{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P{D}_{\ell }P + {g}^{k\ell }{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P{D}_{i}{D}_{\ell }P = {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P.
\]

Now switching derivatives

\[
{D}_{i}{D}_{j}{D}_{k}P = {D}_{i}{D}_{k}{D}_{j}P = {D}_{k}{D}_{i}{D}_{j}P + {R}_{{ikj}\ell }{g}^{\ell m}{D}_{m}P
\]

and if we use this and \( {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} \) and \( {g}^{k\ell }{D}_{\ell }P = {x}^{k} \) we find that

\[
{x}^{k}{D}_{k}{A}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} + {g}^{k\ell }{A}_{ik}{A}_{j\ell } + {R}_{{ikj}\ell }{x}^{k}{x}^{\ell } = 0.
\]

From our assumed curvature bounds we can take \( \left| {R}_{{ijk}\ell }\right|  \leq  {B}_{0} \) . Then we get the following estimate:

\[
\left| {{x}^{k}{D}_{k}{A}_{ij} + {A}_{ij}}\right|  \leq  C{\left| {A}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + C{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

on the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) for some constant \( C \) depending only on the dimension.

We now show how to use the maximum principle on such equations. First of all, by a maximum principle argument, it is easy to show that if \( f \) is a function on a ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) and \( \lambda  > 0 \) is a constant, then

\[
\lambda \sup \left| f\right|  \leq  \sup \left| {{x}^{k}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}^{k}} + {\lambda f}}\right| .
\]

For any tensor \( T = \left\{  {T}_{i\cdots j}\right\} \) and any constant \( \lambda  > 0 \) , setting \( f = {\left| T\right| }^{2} \) in the above inequality, we have

(4.1.8)

\[
\lambda \sup \left| T\right|  \leq  \sup \left| {{x}^{k}{D}_{k}T + {\lambda T}}\right| .
\]

Applying this to the tensor \( {A}_{ij} \) we get

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  C\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}{\left| {A}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + C{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

for some constant depending only on the dimension.

It is fairly elementary to see that there exist constants \( c > 0 \) and \( {C}_{0} < \infty \) such that if the metric \( {g}_{ij} \) is in geodesic coordinates with \( \left| {R}_{{ijk}\ell }\right|  \leq  {B}_{0} \) in the ball of radius \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) then

\[
\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{r}^{2}.
\]

Indeed, since the derivatives of \( {g}_{ij} \) vanish at the origin, so does \( {A}_{ij} \) . Hence the estimate holds near the origin. But the inequality

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  C\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  r}}{\left| {A}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + C{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

says that \( \left| {A}_{ij}\right| \) avoids an interval when \( c \) is chosen small. In fact the inequality

\[
X \leq  C{X}^{2} + D
\]

is equivalent to

\[
\left| {{2CX} - 1}\right|  \geq  \sqrt{1 - {4CD}}
\]

which makes \( X \) avoid an interval if \( {4CD} < 1 \) . (Hence in our case we need to choose \( c \) with \( 4{C}^{2}{c}^{2} < 1 \) .) Then if \( X \) is on the side containing 0 we get

\[
X \leq  \frac{1 - \sqrt{1 - {4CD}}}{2C} \leq  {2D}.
\]

This gives \( \left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{r}^{2} \) with \( {C}_{0} = {2C} \) .

We can also derive bounds on all the covariant derivatives of \( P \) in terms of bounds on the covariant derivatives of the curvature. To simplify the notation, we let

\[
{D}^{q}P = \left\{  {{D}_{{j}_{1}}{D}_{{j}_{2}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}P}\right\}
\]

denote the \( {q}^{\text{ th }} \) covariant derivative, and in estimating \( {D}^{q}P \) we will lump all the lower order terms into a general slush term \( {\Phi }^{q} \) which will be a polynomial in \( {D}^{1}P,{D}^{2}P,\ldots ,{D}^{q - 1}P \) and \( {Rm},{D}^{1}{Rm},\ldots ,{D}^{q - 2}{Rm} \) . We already have estimates on a ball of radius \( r \)

\[
P \leq  {r}^{2}/2
\]

\[
\left| {{D}^{1}P}\right|  \leq  r
\]

\[
\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{r}^{2}
\]

and since \( {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} \) and \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) if we choose \( c \) small we can make

\[
\left| {A}_{ij}\right|  \leq  1/2
\]

and we get

\[
\left| {{D}^{2}P}\right|  \leq  {C}_{2}
\]

for some constant \( {C}_{2} \) depending only on the dimension.

Start with the equation \( {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}P = {2P} \) and apply repeated covariant derivatives. Observe that we get an equation which starts out

\[
{g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}^{q}{D}_{j}P + \cdots  = 0
\]

where the omitted terms only contain derivatives \( {D}^{q}P \) and lower. If we switch two derivatives in a term \( {D}^{q + 1}P \) or lower, we get a term which is a product of a covariant derivative of \( {Rm} \) of order at most \( q - 2 \) (since the two closest to \( P \) commute) and a covariant derivative of \( P \) of order at most \( q - 1 \) ; such a term can be lumped in with the slush term \( {\Phi }^{q} \) . Therefore up to terms in \( {\Phi }^{q} \) we can regard the derivatives as commuting. Then paying attention to the derivatives in \( {D}^{1}P \) we get an equation

\( {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}{D}_{{k}_{1}}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{2}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P \; + {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}{D}_{{k}_{2}}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}{D}_{{k}_{3}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + \cdots  + {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}{D}_{{k}_{q}}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q - 1}}P \; = {D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + {\Phi }^{q}. \)

Recalling that \( {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P = {g}_{ij} + {A}_{ij} \) we can rewrite this as

\[
{\Phi }^{q} = {g}^{ij}{D}_{i}P{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}} + \left( {q - 1}\right) {D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P
\]

\[
+ {g}^{ij}{A}_{i{k}_{1}}{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{2}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q}}P + \cdots  + {g}^{ij}{A}_{i{k}_{q}}{D}_{j}{D}_{{k}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{k}_{q - 1}}P.
\]

Estimating the product of tensors in the usual way gives

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{D}^{q}P + \left( {q - 1}\right) {D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  q\left| A\right| \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  + \left| {\Phi }^{q}\right| .
\]

Applying the inequality \( \lambda \sup \left| T\right|  \leq  \sup \left| {{x}^{k}{D}_{k}T + {\lambda T}}\right| \) with \( T = {D}^{q}P \) gives

\[
\left( {q - 1}\right) \sup \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  \sup \left( {q\left| A\right| \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  + \left| {\Phi }^{q}\right| }\right) .
\]

Now we can make \( \left| A\right|  \leq  1/2 \) by making \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) with \( c \) small; it is important here that \( c \) is independent of \( q \) ! Then we get

\[
\left( {q - 2}\right) \sup \left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  2\sup \left| {\Phi }^{q}\right|
\]

which is a good estimate for \( q \geq  3 \) . The term \( {\Phi }^{q} \) is estimated inductively from the terms \( {D}^{q - 1}P \) and \( {D}^{q - 2}{Rm} \) and lower. This proves that there exist constants \( {C}_{q} \) for \( q \geq  3 \) depending only on \( q \) and the dimension and on \( \left| {{D}^{j}{Rm}}\right| \) for \( j \leq  q - 2 \) such that

\[
\left| {{D}^{q}P}\right|  \leq  {C}_{q}
\]

on the ball \( r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) .

Now we turn our attention to estimating the Euclidean metric \( {I}_{jk} \) and its covariant derivatives with respect to \( {g}_{jk} \) . We will need the following elementary fact: suppose that \( f \) is a function on a ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) with \( f\left( 0\right)  = 0 \) and

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}\frac{\partial f}{\partial {x}^{i}}}\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

for some constant \( C \) . Then

(4.1.9)

\[
\left| f\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

for the same constant \( C \) . As a consequence, if \( T = \left\{  {T}_{j\cdots k}\right\} \) is a tensor which vanishes at the origin and if

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}{D}_{i}T}\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

on a ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \) then \( \left| T\right|  \leq  C{\left| x\right| }^{2} \) with the same constant \( C \) . (Simply apply the inequality (4.1.9) to the function \( f = \left| T\right| \) . In case this is not smooth, we can use \( f = \sqrt{{\left| T\right| }^{2} + {\epsilon }^{2}} - \epsilon \) and then let \( \epsilon  \rightarrow  0 \) .)

Our application will be to the tensor \( {I}_{jk} \) which gives the Euclidean metric as a tensor in geodesic coordinates. We have

\[
{D}_{i}{I}_{jk} =  - {\Gamma }_{ij}^{p}{I}_{pk} - {\Gamma }_{ik}^{p}{I}_{pj}
\]

and since

\[
{x}^{i}{\Gamma }_{ij}^{p} = {g}^{pq}{A}_{jq}
\]

we get the equation

\[
{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{I}_{jk} =  - {g}^{pq}{A}_{jp}{I}_{kq} - {g}^{pq}{A}_{kp}{I}_{jq}.
\]

We already have \( \left| {A}_{jk}\right|  \leq  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2} \) for \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) . The tensor \( {I}_{jk} \) doesn’t vanish at the origin, but the tensor

\[
{h}_{jk} = {I}_{jk} - {g}_{jk}
\]

does. We can then use

\[
{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{h}_{jk} =  - {g}^{pq}{A}_{jp}{h}_{kq} - {g}^{pq}{A}_{kq}{h}_{jq} - 2{A}_{jk}.
\]

Suppose \( M\left( s\right)  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left| x\right|  \leq  s}}\left| {h}_{jk}\right| \) . Then

\[
\left| {{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{h}_{jk}}\right|  \leq  2\left\lbrack  {1 + M\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

and we get

\[
\left| {h}_{jk}\right|  \leq  2\left\lbrack  {1 + M\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

on \( \left| x\right|  \leq  s \) . This makes

\[
M\left( s\right)  \leq  2\left\lbrack  {1 + M\left( s\right) }\right\rbrack  {C}_{0}{B}_{0}{s}^{2}.
\]

Then for \( s \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) with \( c \) small compared to \( {C}_{0} \) we get \( 2{C}_{0}{B}_{0}{s}^{2} \leq  1/2 \) and \( M\left( s\right)  \leq  4{C}_{0}{B}_{0}{s}^{2} \) . Thus

\[
\left| {{I}_{jk} - {g}_{jk}}\right|  = \left| {h}_{jk}\right|  \leq  4{C}_{0}{B}_{0}{\left| x\right| }^{2}
\]

for \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) , and hence for \( c \) small enough

\[
\frac{1}{2}{g}_{jk} \leq  {I}_{jk} \leq  2{g}_{jk}
\]

Thus the metrics are comparable. Note that this estimate only needs \( r \) small compared to \( {B}_{0} \) and does not need any bounds on the derivatives of the curvature.

Now to obtain bounds on the covariant derivative of the Eucliden metric \( {I}_{k\ell } \) with respect to the Riemannian metric \( {g}_{k\ell } \) we want to start with the equation

\[
{x}^{i}{D}_{i}{I}_{k\ell } + {g}^{mn}{A}_{km}{I}_{\ell n} + {g}^{mn}{A}_{\ell m}{I}_{kn} = 0
\]

and apply \( q \) covariant derivatives \( {D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}} \) . Each time we do this we must interchange \( {D}_{j} \) and \( {x}^{i}{D}_{i} \) , and since this produces a term which helps we should look at it closely. If we write \( {R}_{ji} = \left\lbrack  {{D}_{j},{D}_{i}}\right\rbrack \) for the commutator, this operator on tensors involves the curvature but no derivatives. Since

\[
{D}_{j}{x}^{i} = {I}_{j}^{i} + {g}^{im}{A}_{jm}
\]

we can compute

\[
\left\lbrack  {{D}_{j},{x}^{i}{D}_{i}}\right\rbrack   = {D}_{j} + {g}^{im}{A}_{jm}{D}_{i} + {x}^{i}{R}_{ji}
\]

and the term \( {D}_{j} \) in the commutator helps, while \( {A}_{jm} \) can be kept small and \( {R}_{ji} \) is zero order. It follows that we get an equation of the form

\[
0 = {x}^{i}{D}_{i}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell } + q{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }
\]

\[
+ \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{h = 1}}^{q}{g}^{im}{A}_{{j}_{h}m}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{h - 1}}{D}_{i}{D}_{{j}_{h + 1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }
\]

\[
+ {g}^{mn}{A}_{km}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{\ell n} + {g}^{mn}{A}_{\ell m}{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{kn} + {\Psi }^{q},
\]

where the slush term \( {\Psi }^{q} \) is a polynomial in derivatives of \( {I}_{k\ell } \) of degree no more than \( q - 1 \) and derivatives of \( P \) of degree no more than \( q + 2 \) (remember \( {x}^{i} = {g}^{ij}{D}_{j}P \) and \( {A}_{ij} = {D}_{i}{D}_{j}P - {g}_{ij} \) ) and derivatives of the curvature \( {Rm} \) of degree no more than \( q - 1 \) . We now estimate

\[
{D}^{q}{I}_{k\ell } = \left\{  {{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }}\right\}
\]

by induction on \( q \) using (4.1.8) with \( \lambda  = q \) . Noticing a total of \( q + 2 \) terms contracting \( {A}_{ij} \) with a derivative of \( {I}_{k\ell } \) of degree \( q \) , we get the estimate

\[
q\sup \left| {{D}^{q}{I}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  \left( {q + 2}\right) \sup \left| A\right| \sup \left| {{D}^{q}{I}_{k\ell }}\right|  + \sup \left| {\Psi }^{q}\right| .
\]

and everything works. This proves that there exists a constant \( c > 0 \) depending only on the dimension, and constants \( {C}_{q} \) depending only on the dimension and \( q \) and bounds \( {B}_{j} \) on the curvature and its derivatives for \( j \leq  q \) where \( \left| {{D}^{j}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {B}_{j} \) , so that for any metric \( {g}_{k\ell } \) in geodesic coordinates in the ball \( \left| x\right|  \leq  r \leq  c/\sqrt{{B}_{0}} \) the Euclidean metric \( {I}_{k\ell } \) satisfies

\[
\frac{1}{2}{g}_{k\ell } \leq  {I}_{k\ell } \leq  2{g}_{k\ell }
\]

and the covariant derivatives of \( {I}_{k\ell } \) with respect to \( {g}_{k\ell } \) satisfy

\[
\left| {{D}_{{j}_{1}}\cdots {D}_{{j}_{q}}{I}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  {C}_{q}.
\]

The difference between a covariant derivative and an ordinary derivative is given by the connection

\[
- {\Gamma }_{ij}^{p}{I}_{pk} - {\Gamma }_{ik}^{p}{I}_{pj}
\]

to get

\[
{\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} = \frac{1}{2}{I}^{k\ell }\left( {{D}_{\ell }{I}_{ij} - {D}_{i}{I}_{j\ell } - {D}_{j}{I}_{i\ell }}\right) .
\]

This gives us bounds on \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) . We then obtain bounds on the first derivatives of \( {g}_{ij} \) from

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{i}}{g}_{jk} = {g}_{k\ell }{\Gamma }_{ij}^{\ell } + {g}_{j\ell }{\Gamma }_{ik}^{\ell }.
\]

Always proceeding inductively on the order of the derivative, we now get bounds on covariant derivatives of \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) from the covariant derivatives of \( {I}_{pk} \) and bounds of the ordinary derivatives of \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) by relating the to the covariant derivatives using the \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{k} \) , and bounds on the ordinary derivatives of the \( {g}_{jk} \) from bounds on the ordinary derivatives of the \( {\Gamma }_{ij}^{\ell } \) . Consequently, we have estimates

\[
\frac{1}{2}{I}_{k\ell } \leq  {g}_{k\ell } \leq  2{I}_{k\ell }
\]

and

\[
\left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{1}}}\cdots \frac{\partial }{\partial {x}^{{j}_{q}}}{g}_{k\ell }}\right|  \leq  {\widetilde{C}}_{q}
\]

for similar constants \( {\widetilde{C}}_{q} \) .

Therefore we have finished the proof of Claim 1.

knowledge_statements.title: Topology Induced by a Differentiable Atlas
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topology Induced by a Differentiable Atlas
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A differentiable structure on a set \( M \) induces a natural topology on \( M \) . It suffices to define \( A \subset  M \) to be an open set in \( M \) if and only if \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }^{-1}\left( {A \cap  {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right) }\right) \) is an open set in \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) for all \( \alpha \) . It is easy to verify that \( M \) and the empty set are open sets, that a union of open sets is again an open set and that the finite intersection of open sets remains an open set. Observe that the topology is defined in such a way that the sets \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha }\left( {U}_{\alpha }\right) \) are open and that the mappings \( {\mathbf{x}}_{\alpha } \) are continuous.

The Euclidean space \( {\mathbf{R}}^{n} \) , with the differentiable structure given by the identity, is a trivial example of a differentiable manifold. Now we shall see a non-trivial example.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
. For every \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) we can find \( \sigma  < \infty \) such that \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  \varepsilon \) for \( s \geq  \sigma \) . The curvature tensor evolves by a formula

\[
{D}_{t}{Rm} = {\Delta Rm} + {Rm} * {Rm}
\]

which gives a formula

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} = \Delta {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| DRm\right| }^{2} + {Rm} * {Rm} * {Rm}
\]

and an estimate

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} + C{\left| Rm\right| }^{3}
\]

for some constant \( C \) depending only on the dimension. For any \( \delta  > 0 \) choose

\[
\rho  = \sigma  + \left( {{M}^{2} - {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) /\delta
\]

and choose the continuous function

\[
\psi  = \left\{  \begin{array}{lll} {M}^{2} & \text{ if } & s \leq  \sigma , \\  {M}^{2} - \delta \left( {s - \sigma }\right)  = {\varepsilon }^{2} + \delta \left( {\rho  - s}\right) & \text{ if } & \sigma  \leq  s \leq  \rho , \\  {\varepsilon }^{2} & \text{ if } & s \geq  \rho . \end{array}\right.
\]

where \( s \) is the distance from some origin at \( t = 0 \) . Then \( \psi \) is Lipschitz continuous since \( s \) is, and since \( \left| {Ds}\right|  \leq  1 \) almost everywhere we also have \( \left| {D\psi }\right|  \leq  \delta \) almost everywhere.

Now we can smooth \( \psi \) locally and patch together with a partition of unity to get a function \( \widetilde{\psi } \) which is smooth and has

\[
- {\varepsilon }^{2} \leq  \widetilde{\psi } \leq  {M}^{2} + {\varepsilon }^{2}\;\text{ and }\;\left| {D\widetilde{\psi }}\right|  \leq  {2\delta }\;\text{ everywhere }
\]

and

\[
\widetilde{\psi } \geq  {M}^{2} - {\varepsilon }^{2}\;\text{ for }\;s \leq  \sigma \;\text{ and }\;\widetilde{\psi } \leq  {\varepsilon }^{2}\;\text{ if }\;s \geq  \rho .
\]

Lastly take \( \varphi  = \psi  + 2{\varepsilon }^{2} \) . Then

\[
{\varepsilon }^{2} \leq  \varphi  \leq  {M}^{2} + 3{\varepsilon }^{2}\;\text{ and }\;\left| {D\varphi }\right|  \leq  {2\delta }\;\text{ everywhere }
\]

and

\[
\varphi  \geq  {M}^{2}\text{ if }s \leq  \sigma \text{ and }\varphi  \leq  3{\varepsilon }^{2}\text{ if }s \geq  \rho .
\]

Now define \( \varphi \) for \( t \geq  0 \) by solving the scalar heat equation

\[
\frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial t} = {\Delta \varphi }
\]

in the Laplacian of the metric evolving by the Ricci Flow. By the maximum principle we still have \( {\varepsilon }^{2} \leq  \varphi  \leq  {M}^{2} \) everywhere for \( t \geq  0 \) . The derivative \( {D}_{a}\varphi \) evolves in an evolving orthonormal frame by the formula

\[
{D}_{t}{D}_{a}\varphi  = \Delta {D}_{a}\varphi
\]

and hence

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| D\varphi \right| }^{2} = \Delta {\left| D\varphi \right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {D}^{2}\varphi \right| }^{2}.
\]

Note this formula does not involve the curvature. Hence \( \left| {D\varphi }\right|  \leq  {2\delta } \) everywhere for \( t \geq  0 \) by the maximum principle.

The second derivative \( {D}_{a}{D}_{b}\varphi \) evolves by the formula

\[
{D}_{t}{D}_{a}{D}_{b}\varphi  = \Delta {D}_{a}{D}_{b}\varphi  + 2{R}_{acbd}{D}_{c}{D}_{d}\varphi
\]

and hence

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {D}^{2}\varphi \right| }^{2} = \Delta {\left| {D}^{2}\varphi \right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {D}^{3}\varphi \right| }^{2} + 4{R}_{acbd}{D}_{a}{D}_{b}\varphi {D}_{c}{D}_{d}\varphi
\]

which gives an estimate

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {D}^{2}\varphi \right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| {D}^{2}\varphi \right| }^{2} + {CM}{\left| {D}^{2}\varphi \right| }^{2}
\]

for some constant \( C \) depending only on the dimension. Let us put

\[
F = t{\left| {D}^{2}\varphi \right| }^{2} + {\left| D\varphi \right| }^{2}
\]

and compute

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} \leq  {\Delta F} - \left( {1 - {CMt}}\right) {\left| {D}^{2}\varphi \right| }^{2}.
\]

Then if \( t \leq  c/M \) where \( c = 1/C \) depends only on the dimension, we have

\[
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} \leq  {\Delta F}
\]

and the maximum of \( F \) decreases. But

\[
F \leq  4{\delta }^{2}
\]

at \( t = 0 \) , and hence for \( t \geq  0 \) also. Thus

\[
\left| {{D}^{2}\varphi }\right|  \leq  {2\delta }/\sqrt{t}\;\text{ for }\;0 < t \leq  c/M.
\]

Since \( {\left| \Delta \varphi \right| }^{2} \leq  n{\left| {D}^{2}\varphi \right| }^{2} \) and \( \varphi \) solves the heat equation,

\[
\left| \frac{\partial \varphi }{\partial t}\right|  \leq  {C\delta }\sqrt{t}\text{ for }0 < t \leq  c/M
\]

where this constant \( C = 2\sqrt{n} \) depends only on the dimension \( n \) . Now \( 1/\sqrt{t} \) has an improper integral which is \( 2\sqrt{t} \) which is finite, so for all \( P \)

\[
\left| {\varphi \left( {P, t}\right)  - \varphi \left( {P,0}\right) }\right|  \leq  {2C\delta }\sqrt{t}\text{ for }0 < t \leq  c/M.
\]

Since \( \delta  > 0 \) is arbitrarily small, we can take

\[
\delta  \leq  {\varepsilon }^{2}\sqrt{M}/{2C}\sqrt{c}
\]

so that \( {2C\delta }\sqrt{t} \leq  {\varepsilon }^{2} \) for \( t \leq  c/M \) . Then \( \varphi  \leq  4{\varepsilon }^{2} \) at times \( t \leq  c/M \) on the set where \( s \geq  \rho \) at \( t = 0 \) . Now distances can expand, but only at an exponential rate governed by \( M \) . In particular if \( s = s\left( {P,0, t}\right) \) is the distance between a point \( P \) and the origin 0 at time \( t \) , we have

\[
\frac{\partial s}{\partial t} \leq  {CMs}
\]

and

\[
s\left( t\right)  \leq  s\left( 0\right) {e}^{CMt}.
\]

This gives us a constant \( C \) depending only on the dimension such that if \( s \geq  {C\rho } \) at \( P \) at time \( t \leq  c/M \) then \( s \geq  \rho \) at \( P \) at \( t = 0 \) , and \( \varphi  \leq  4{\epsilon }^{2} \) at \( P \) at time \( t \) .

Now at \( t = 0 \) we have

\[
{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  {M}^{2} \leq  \varphi \text{ if }s \leq  \sigma
\]

and

\[
{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  {\varepsilon }^{2} \leq  \varphi \text{ if }s \geq  \sigma
\]

so \( {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \varphi \) everywhere at \( t = 0 \) . Since

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} + C{\left| Rm\right| }^{3}
\]

we have

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} + {CM}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

while

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {{e}^{CMt}\varphi }\right)  = \Delta \left( {{e}^{CMt}\varphi }\right)  + {CM}\left( {{e}^{CMt}\varphi }\right)
\]

so \( {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  {e}^{CMt}\varphi \) by the maximum principle. For \( t \leq  c/M \) this gives \( {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq \; {C\varphi } \) for some other constant \( C \) depending only on the dimension. Hence at time \( t \) we have

\[
{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  C{\varepsilon }^{2}\text{ for }s \geq  {C\rho }
\]

where these constants \( C \) depend only on the dimension and are independent of \( \varepsilon \) . Thus \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \rightarrow  0 \) for \( t \leq  c/M \) also as \( s \rightarrow  \infty \) . Since the time interval can always be advanced by \( c/M \) as long as \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  M \) , we get the result until \( \left| {Rm}\right| \) becomes unbounded or \( t \rightarrow  \infty \) .

knowledge_statements.title: Fine versus Coarse Ricci-Flow Estimates
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fine versus Coarse Ricci-Flow Estimates
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
1.1. The distinction between fine and coarse estimates. It is useful to distinguish between what we may call fine estimates with what we may call coarse estimates. Since we apply these terminologies in a casual way, we describe our distinction between them in terms of examples. Examples of fine estimates in the theory of Ricci flow are curvature pinching estimates, Harnack-type estimates, entropy formulas, and monotonicity formulas. We may decree that an aspect of the fineness of an estimate is its sensitivity to perturbation. \( {}^{1} \) Although the matrix and trace Harnack estimates for the Ricci flow are known assuming nonnegative curvature operator in dimensions 2 and above, so far no substantial improvements (i.e., perturbations) seem to be known for dimensions 3 and above (in dimension 2 there is a trace Harnack estimate for arbitrary solutions on closed surfaces). On the other hand, one may think of the Hamilton-Ivey curvature estimate as a perturbation of the 'nonnegative sectional curvature is preserved' estimate in dimension 3. In this sense Harnack-type estimates appear finer than curvature pinching estimates although an analogy exists between them via the space-time approach. \( {}^{2} \) A further comment is that curvature pinching estimates in dimension 3 may be thought of as (large) perturbations of the 'nonnegative sectional (or Ricci) curvature is preserved' estimate.

Another aspect of the fineness of an estimate is how sharp it is; in general, finer estimates are sharper. A classical sharp example in Riemannian geometry is the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison theorem. In the Ricci flow, the matrix Harnack estimate is sharp (i.e., equality is attained in certain directions) on expanding gradient Ricci solitons. Moreover, for the corresponding Harnack estimate for ancient solutions we have that equality is attained on steady gradient Ricci solitons. Strikingly, Perelman has proved sharp monotonicity formulas for complete solutions of the Ricci flow on both closed and noncompact manifolds (without curvature sign restrictions). These estimates are sharp, as are monotonicity formulas in geometric flows in general.

On the other hand, in deriving coarse estimates, the ability to successfully apply the maximum principle to the evolution equations of the relevant quantities does not depend in a sensitive way on the constants in these quantities. For this reason we consider the global and local derivative of curvature estimates to be coarse estimates. Perhaps for the same reason derivative estimates hold for a number of different geometric evolution equations besides the Ricci flow including the heat equation on Riemannian manifolds and the mean curvature flow.

---

\( {}^{1} \) That is, the finer the estimate, the more difficult it is to perturb.

\( {}^{2} \) However, the reader may argue that a Harnack estimate in dimension \( n \) corresponds to a curvature estimate in dimension \( n + 1 \) since time adds a dimension, so that the apparent increase in fineness really corresponds to an increase in dimension.

---

The fineness or coarseness of an estimate may not be related to its relative importance to the study of a geometric flow; however, it may be related to its geometric significance. We venture to say that, in general, finer estimates are positively correlated to more geometrically significant estimates. An example of what we mean by this is that in many monotonicity formulas, the equality case, i.e., the case where the geometric invariant is constant under the flow, is characterized as occurring if and only if the solution is self-similar.
